title: Why has Waymo pulled all its driverless cars from US freeways?
text:
Waymo has temporarily suspended driverless rides on US freeways after California banned the service over safety concerns.

California's Department of Motor Vehicles said a series of traffic incidents, including robotaxis entering active construction zones, posed an imminent risk to public safety. Waymo has now restricted freeway operations in all other US markets while it reviews the performance of its vehicles.

Waymo currently operates in 15 US cities, though only offered driverless freeway rides in a handful of cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.

title: The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires
text:
In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.

The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.

Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at between $70 - $78 each.

If they go for the highest price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $18.5bn each.

So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?

In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.

He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.

Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track , and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.

Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.

Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.

But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.

Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".

Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.

She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.

Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.

She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.

The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.

Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.

He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.

Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.

He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".

Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.

Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.

Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.

He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.

Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.

Jared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.

He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University.

His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic.

Chris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other.

But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum.

Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI.

He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain.

The Canadian left the University of Toronto early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.

Sam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.

McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.

He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.

title: The Avinox Motor Disrupted e-MTB. Now It’s Coming for Your Commute.
author: Josh Ross
text:
This week, Amflow is expanding beyond electric mountain bikes with the launch of its first city commuter line, the Amflow UE Series. On the surface, it sounds like yet another unfamiliar name offering a high-powered commuter bike, but the news is a bit bigger than that. What this really means is that DJI-backed Amflow and its Avinox motor are making the jump from e-MTB to city riding.

Available now in the UE Carbon and UE Carbon Pro builds, the platform pairs that drive system with a claimed 2.35-kilogram full-carbon, low step-through frame to hit a complete bike weight of 20.9 kilograms, or roughly 46 pounds. It makes for an impressive offering on paper and raises the obvious question of whether putting that kind of hardware into a transportation-focused package will reshape the commuter market the same way Amflow did e-MTB.

Rather than offering a traditional multi-size run at launch, Amflow designed the standard UE frame to accommodate riders between 5 feet, 1 inch and 6 feet, 3 inches using two interchangeable stem heights. A dedicated small frame for riders between 4 feet, 7 inches and 5 feet, 3 inches is scheduled to arrive in 2027.

Beyond that, the bike follows expected commuter design patterns, leaning toward comfort and visibility. The first lever of that focus is frame geometry, starting with a step-through frame and flat handlebars to put the rider in an upright position. That layout is paired with 65 mm of front suspension, a seatpost with 125 mm of height adjustment and 30 mm of suspension travel, and wide 26×2.0-inch Maxxis tires. Braking comes from Magura 180 mm disc brakes with three-finger levers. For hauling cargo, Amflow equips the bike with a front rack rated for 20 kilograms (about 44 pounds) and a rear MIK HD-compatible rack rated for 27 kilograms (about 59.5 pounds).

The biggest news here is that the motor that disrupted the e-MTB market is expanding into new territory. Powering both builds is the Avinox M2 drive unit, which Amflow claims delivers up to 125 Nm of torque and an 8-to-1 maximum assist ratio. According to the brand, the motor can climb 30% grades under load while keeping operating noise below 45 dBA. The system also includes a traction control feature and a new Auto Boost mode that automatically increases power output on steep hills or loaded starts without rider input.

Both builds use a removable 600Wh battery, with Amflow claiming a maximum range of 132 kilometers (about 82 miles) under controlled testing conditions. It charges from zero to 100% in 2 hours and 23 minutes, and riders can set a custom charge limit to preserve cell longevity.

Both models also feature electronic shifting with automatic and smooth-shifting modes, leaving the drivetrain as the main mechanical difference between the two. The UE Carbon Pro uses a custom three-speed electronic internal geared hub paired with a Gates carbon belt, which allows riders to shift while stopped and avoids chain maintenance or greasy clothes — though it costs more. Alternatively, the less expensive Amflow UE Carbon uses a 10-speed electronic rear derailleur co-developed with TRP.

Amflow leans heavily into its connected ecosystem on the UE Series, integrating several new Avinox accessories directly into the bike. Control centers on a 1.4-inch DP200 handlebar touchscreen paired with a rotating phone mount that offers 15W wireless and 20W USB-C charging. The integrated lighting system features automatic dusk activation, high- and low-beam switching and a brake-sensing rear light.

Through the Avinox Ride app, riders can pair multiple bikes to one account, merge ride files, sync with an Apple Watch and control compatible DJI Osmo cameras from the handlebar. The system can also pair with a heart rate monitor to adjust motor assist automatically based on a target heart rate zone.

On the security front, a single key operates both the battery lock and an integrated 10 mm hardened steel ART 2-Star horseshoe lock. The bike also supports Apple Find My tracking and an app-based Lost Mode designed to disable the bike remotely if it is stolen.

Both the Amflow UE Carbon and UE Carbon Pro are available immediately through Amflow’s website and authorized dealers. U.S. pricing is $3,499 for the UE Carbon and $3,899 for the UE Carbon Pro.

title: Florida pastor found guilty over 2021 assassination of Haitian president
author: Associated Press
text:
Christian Emmanuel Sanon faces life in prison after conviction on charges arising from killing of Jovenel Moïse

A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted on Wednesday of US charges arising from the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse.

Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on charges including conspiring to kill Moïse after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami . He had faced a total of eight charges including conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.

He faces up to life in prison at sentencing.

Federal prosecutors said south Florida was a hub for planning and financing the plot to oust Moïse and install a president of the conspirators’ choosing. The government said Sanon was the conspirators’ initial choice for Moïse’s replacement. Prosecutors also said Sanon helped raise money for the conspiracy and arranged travel to Haiti and lodging for himself and others in that country.

Sanon acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moïse, but pointed out that the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill Moïse.

Sanon was born in Haiti and moved to the US as a teenager. He testified that he worked with churches in Haitian immigrant communities in Florida and the midwest.

Haiti has not had a president since authorities said that a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers killed Moïse and wounded his wife in a night-time raid at their home on 7 July 2021. The poorest country in the Americas , Haiti has a history of dictatorship, political upheaval and foreign intervention that has long hindered democratic rule.

The election of a new president is scheduled for next year.

Prosecutors said the scheme to kill Moïse included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from US government programs that were intended to help businesses during the Covid pandemic, according to court records. US prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences.

The plot to oust Moïse began taking final shape in April 2021, when Sanon met in south Florida with a former Haitian senator and several US businesspeople, according to an indictment. The group agreed that Sanon, once in power, would award contracts to two Florida-based companies – Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security, collectively known as CTU – for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment, according to investigators.

CTU initially hired about 18 Colombian nationals with military training to provide security for Sanon, according to prosecutors. Conspirators also spent months obtaining weapons and body armor and attempting to build ties with Haitian gangs, officials said.

By June 2021, the conspirators realized Sanon had neither the constitutional qualifications nor sufficient popular support to become president. They shifted their support to Wendelle Coq Thélot, a former Haitian supreme court judge who died in January 2025 while a fugitive.

Sanon was previously scheduled to be tried with four other men who were convicted earlier this year, but his case was separated from theirs and delayed for health reasons.

title: Manchester United’s infamous 1974 relegation is a warning from history
author: Sam Cunningham
text:
It may have been a different era, but the 1970s contain salutary lessons for a club in serious decline once again

I n many ways, there are striking parallels between the Manchester United relegated in 1974 and the Manchester United sitting in the relegation zone at this stage of the season for the first time in 40 years. A legendary manager leaves, his shadow remains; with boardroom dithering and uncertainty, his replacements churn and burn as the club slide over several years.

Sir Matt Busby stepped aside as manager of the 1968 European Cup-winning side, but stayed on as a director, just as Sir Alex Ferguson did, watching from the Old Trafford directors’ box as successors tried and failed.

In the six years after being crowned kings of Europe, United turned to Wilf McGuinness, Busby stepped in temporarily to keep them up, then Frank O’Farrell was appointed before they landed on Tommy Docherty, who experienced the ignominy of taking them down.

In the past eight years, United have sacked José Mourinho, Ole Gunnar Solskjær, Erik ten Hag , Ruben Amorim and now Michael Carrick .

How did the United of 1974 go down? Most outsiders believed they were too big to fail. Inside the club, though, they sensed the direction of travel. After a heavy defeat at Crystal Palace in December 1972, Busby offered Docherty the job in the Selhurst Park boardroom. “There’s a lot of trouble in the camp,” Busby said. Docherty was doing well as Scotland manager and took a few days to mull it over, but decided he couldn’t turn down the opportunity.

When Busby called him on the Sunday evening, he accepted. “You know it won’t be easy?” Busby said. “It’ll be like turning an oil tanker round, only bigger.” He added: “You might find yourself having to take a step back in order to take a leap forward.” Docherty wrote in his autobiography, The Doc, that at the time he never believed Busby was alluding to relegation.

Docherty was given free rein for a rebuild. The day after his appointment, he signed George Graham from Arsenal for £120,000, a sizeable fee at the time. Alex Forsyth followed from Partick for £100,000 and Docherty pulled off a coup when he persuaded Lou Macari to join bottom-of-the-table United instead of Liverpool for £200,000.

The giants of the previous era were moved on. In February, Bobby Charlton told him that, at 37, it would be his last season. Other big names wanted to stay, but Docherty felt a reset was needed. “The Manchester United team that had won the European Cup in 1968 was without a doubt a great team, but many members of that side had been allowed to grow old together,” he wrote.

“I knew what I had decided would prove very unpopular with many people but it had to be done. I set out my stall to end the United careers of among others Denis Law, Tony Dunne, Pat Crerand and David Sadler.”

George Best, who had retired once but returned under Docherty, played his last game on New Year’s Day 1974 after repeatedly turning up late. The most controversial departure was Law, who was allowed to join Manchester City.

Having taken over with United bottom, Docherty kept them up in his first season and was emboldened to continue his clearout. Thirteen players were released that summer. But halfway through the following season they were facing relegation again and a lack of goals cost them. At one stage, the joint-top scorer was Alex Stepney, with two penalties. He was the goalkeeper.

Relegation was confirmed on the penultimate day as they lost to City, a defeat made all the more painful by Law back-heeling the late winner. Docherty was interviewed on the Old Trafford pitch and asked, in a scene replayed in TNT Sports’ Too Good To Go Down, whether the club would drift into obscurity. “No, there’s no danger,” he said. “We could wash the jerseys here and hang them out to dry and you’d get 15,000 people standing watching them do so.”

Despite the bravado, Docherty was expecting the sack when he met Busby a few days later. Instead, Busby handed him a case of champagne, reminded him of the oil tanker and told him to set to work getting them back up.

Docherty’s prediction proved right: the brand was far bigger than the division they played in. In the Second Division, Old Trafford averaged crowds of more than 47,000 – the biggest in the country – and their away support descended on towns and cities and routinely outnumbered the home contingent.

Docherty bought young and hungry, targeting players with a point to prove, including Steve Coppell from Tranmere, Stuart Pearson from Hull and Jim Holton from Shrewsbury. The direct, attacking football synonymous with United returned and the Scot shaped a fearless 4-2-4 formation.

Crowds grew after they came straight back up and for a while United were on course to become the fifth side to win the First Division after promotion, but finished third and also reached the FA Cup final, losing 1-0 to Southampton. That shows the stark differences between then and now.

The gap between the first and second tiers was narrower. United did not lose a gargantuan broadcast deal when they went down. They were not saddled with debt by their owners. Their wage bill was not tied to Champions League qualification. Players were not on long contracts and were easier to buy and sell. There were no disruptive agents. Fans were more patient.

If lessons of the 1970s are not heeded soon, the fallout could be infinitely more painful.

title: Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
text:
It was during November 2020 that somewhere in San Francisco, a woman called Daniela Amodei phoned a friend, asking for advice.

Daniela oversaw safety and policy at OpenAI, one of the most talked-about AI companies in the world.

But Daniela and her brother Dario - who worked there too - had misgivings over safety levels at OpenAI and thought it could be time to walk away.

So she did what many do when we can't make a decision about something, she phoned a friend. The friend's reply was direct and to the point: "You don't need to be on the phone with me. You already know the answer."

The Amodei siblings and a handful of other colleagues quit. Together, they set up a rival – Anthropic.

Six years on and Anthropic, the maker of leading AI model Claude, has predicted revenues of $52bn in 2026 and $135bn in 2027, according to analyst estimates.

It is about to sell shares to the public for the first time in what's known as an Initial Public Offering or IPO, aiming for a valuation of an estimated $1.4tn (£1tn), which would propel it straight into the top 10 of the most valuable US companies.

The sale comes at a crucial time when many are wondering whether, amid increasing concern about the potential of AI, the industry's bubble is showing signs of bursting.

Where once investors were "all in" on a technological revolution to rival the railroads, the car, electricity and the internet, some are now hedging their bets, amid arguments that AI prices will be driven down as the technology becomes more common and concerns that a hefty wedge of the AI investment is tech giants investing in each other.

Shares in companies that supply the raw computing power behind AI, like Coreweave and Nebius, have seen their value cut in half while even the mighty Nvidia has lost its crown as the world's most valuable company with its shares down 30% - a staggering $2tn fall in value.

So could the Anthropic IPO reinflate the bubble or will it be remembered as the last gasp of a boom that is heading for a bust?

At an event last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told JPMorgan Chase's CEO Jamie Dimon that his guiding principle was to "never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it's worth".

The company is selling roughly $65bn worth of shares to the general public and a further $26bn on to other big tech companies. It is comfortably the single biggest money raising event in US corporate history.

It's an old adage that during a gold rush you should buy companies that sell the picks and shovels as opposed to those staking everything on striking gold. In AI's case that's the chip makers, the data centre builders, the energy providers. But Anthropic is arguably the gold itself and this IPO will see what value people put on it, according to Fiona Cincotta.

"I think the reason that this IPO is so important is basically it's the first ability for the public investors to access a pure play AI trade," she says, adding that previous offerings have been about "other parts of the ecosystem, which are, the semiconductors, the chips, the, data centres. But this is the first time that we were actually able to access the AI provider."

What a company is worth depends almost entirely on predicted future earnings.

It's that calculation that many think presents the sharpest needle to the AI bubble.

Will current and future users of AI be prepared to pay enough to justify the trillions being spent on the chips, data centres, energy and employees, some of whom can command annual salaries of over $100m?

"AI is certainly in a financial bubble. While LLMs [large language models] offer genuine utility and are undoubtedly here to stay, the economics don't add up," said Gary Marcus, Professor Emeritus at New York University and author of Taming Silicon Valley, speaking earlier this year.

"[The] more companies build AI models, the [more the] technology becomes commoditised, eliminating meaningful competitive advantages and driving down prices."

So far, the growth rates in Anthropic revenue are extraordinary.

But these explosive growth rates hide a potential problem. Around a quarter of that revenue came from just a handful of companies, among them Google and Amazon.

It's also concentrated in the US which accounts for two-thirds of its revenue.

There is also the staggering network of circular financing found in the AI world. For example, Anthropic has agreements to buy or lease hundreds of billions of dollars worth of chips and computing power from a handful of companies including Broadcom, Google, Amazon. Many of those firms are also investors in Anthropic and major customers of its products.

It's not just some Wall Street investors questioning whether the AI boom is all it's cracked up to be. Out on Main Street, ordinary Americans have concerns too.

With the US driving so much of global AI growth, a growing public backlash against a technology that threatens to replace millions of jobs and hoover up vast amounts of energy and water became a factor in the recent midterm elections in the US.

Many areas in the US have passed moratoriums on data centre development and many candidates deemed too close to big tech found that association a political liability rather than an asset. Many Democrat candidates publicly opposed data centre development and won.

Added to that, the Pied Piper of AI, chip maker Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang, resigned last week after admitting to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.

Huang's spectacular fall from grace and Nvidia's 30% fall in value from its peak have left AI investors looking for a new champion for the AI boom that has underpinned the US stock market and arguably much of its entire economy for the last two years.

If Anthropic – and its CEO are to be AI's new Pied Piper, he will be playing a different tune to the relentlessly upbeat, leather jacket-clad talisman Huang.…

title: Bottas' stay at Cadillac confirmed for 2027
text:
Valtteri Bottas has been retained by Cadillac for the 2027 Formula 1 season.

The future of the 37-year-old Finn had been in doubt as the American team endure a difficult maiden campaign.

To date, they have failed to collect a point in either the drivers' or constructors' championship.

However, two-time championship runner-up Bottas will race again with them next year.

"I'm excited to continue this journey with Cadillac into 2027," said Bottas, who is preparing for Sunday's Las Vegas Grand Prix.

"We knew building a new Formula One team from the ground up wasn't going to be easy, but that's exactly what makes this challenge so special.

"We've laid the foundations, we're learning and improving, and there's still plenty more to come. I'm hungry for more, and I believe in what we're building together. The story is only just getting started."

The news follows the recent announcement that Mexican Sergio Perez, 36, will also be remaining with Cadillac until 2029 after signing a contract extension.

Cadillac had been considering whether to promote their American reserve driver, Colton Herta, into Bottas' seat.

The 26-year-old former Indycar driver has earned enough points to apply for the superlicence required to drive in F1 through his outings in practice this year.

But the feeling was that there was no obvious upgrade to Bottas and that the Finn had not been given a fair run in what has been a difficult debut season for Cadillac beset by reliability problems and lack of pace.

The team decided that they needed stability for their second season, and that the experience provided by Perez and Bottas, who have both won grands prix, was as important as ever.

Herta had given up his seat in Indycar to drive in Formula 2 this season with the idea of preparing himself for F1.

However, he has had a difficult season and lies 19th in the championship with two races remaining.

Herta now faces a decision as to what to do in 2027.

Cadillac are still open to the idea of him graduating to F1, perhaps in 2028, but it is not clear where he may race next year while he waits to see whether that opportunity arises.

TWG, the US consortium which runs Cadillac, has other teams in other categories for which Herta could race alongside any F1 reserve role that might be on offer.

One of the options would involve a return to Indycar, or Herta could perhaps move into endurance racing.

Whatever happened to the diamond that went missing in F1 crash?

Cowboy boots, cocktails and casinos - how do three US grands prix compare?

title: The longest single-opponent winning streaks in Knicks history
author: Michael Zeno
text:
On Tuesday night, the Knicks outlasted the Raptors for the second time in three nights to extend a staggering 15-game winning streak against their Canadian rivals that dates back to January 2023.

Beyond the fact that it means that old friends RJ Barrett and Immanuel Quickley have never beaten their old team, it also extends one of the longest streaks in program history against a single opponent.

Celtics, 21 games (1993-98)

As mentioned on last night’s broadcast, it’s hard to believe such a dominant stretch existed against a longtime rival that has been the Eastern Conference’s banner of success for generations.

Simply, the sport is cyclical, and the few times the Celtics were in the doldrums, the Knicks were contending for titles. Through the many dark ages of Knicks history, the Celtics dominated. It’s why they’ve only faced off in the postseason three times in the last 35 years.

From 1965-67, the Celtics won 21 in a row against the Knicks in the heart of the Bill Russell era. It took 25 years to return the favor.

On January 10, 1993, the Celtics outlasted the Knicks at TD Garden in a 100-97 win. They wouldn’t win another game in this rivalry for over five years.

The Celtics won 48 games in 1992-93, but quickly fell into the East’s cellar. They wouldn’t win 40 games again in a season until 2001-02, while at the same time, Patrick Ewing and the Knicks had only the Bulls and Pacers competing with them for spots in the NBA Finals yearly.

Ewing would score 65 combined over the next two meetings in April 1993 before scoring 30 again on Opening Night that October in a three-point win in Boston. He routinely owned the Celtics during this time, reaching a crescendo with a 36-14 effort in March 1994.

As the Celtics got worse, the Knicks took advantage of them more and more. A 35-point blowout in February 1994 still stands as one of the biggest blowouts in the rivalry’s history. Hubert Davis nailed five threes and scored 25 points in a 90-83 win the following month.

It was always a different enemy that flummoxed the Celtics. Charles Smith scoring 25, Anthony Mason scoring 21, and John Starks and Ewing’s consistency. Even as Pat Riley turned into Jeff Van Gundy, the Knicks never lost a step.

The streak had reached 17 by January 28, 1997, when the pitiful 9-30 Celtics put the greatest scare into the contending Knicks yet. An eight-point lead in the final minutes dwindled to a tie on a Todd Day three in the final minute before free throws by Antoine Walker gave Boston the lead in the final minute.

Just when the streak appeared over, Chris Childs called game with eight seconds left.

Eventually, the streak would finally end on January 26, 1998, when the Knicks were held to just 85 points behind a 25-point gem by Chauncey Billups. Even this triumphant victory came with an asterisk, as Ewing missed the game due to wrist surgery. Huh.

Cavaliers, 18 games (1980-83)

The Knicks own the Cavs in the playoffs, but did you know there was a stretch they owned them like

In five all-time playoff meetings, the Knicks are 16-2 against the Cavs, but once took things to another level in the early 1980s.

Unlike the Celtics, this is pretty peculiar. The Knicks were an average team during this streak, but took advantage of one of the worst eras of Cavs basketball under Ted Stepien.

Quite precisely, this streak can be known as the “Stepien Streak”, as while he was owner from April 1980 to his sale in April 1983, the Cavs went 1-16 against the Knicks, with the lone win coming just two weeks before he sold the team in late March of 1983.

Highlights of the streak include Mike Glenn’s 29-point game in November 1980 (second-highest scoring game of his career), Ray Williams’ 37-point gem in an overtime win two weeks later, and perennially playing in front of 4,000 fans at an empty Richfield Coliseum. The NBA was totally different in the 80s.

Bullets, 17 games (1952-53)

Back in the day, there weren’t many teams. As such, you get stuff like this.

Over a span of 400 days from February 6, 1952, to March 11, 1953, the Knicks played the Baltimore Bullets 17 times and won every single one of them.

The 1950s Knicks can sometimes be referred to as the Silver Era of Knicks basketball due to the team making multiple Finals appearances before Russell came and made the East his own, so it’s no surprise they were dominant. But like this?

The lore of 1950s NBA is quite fascinating. These teams played each other three times in six days in February 1952 when the streak began, but played the games in three different places. The Bullets won 82-81 in the Baltimore Coliseum on February 4, the Knicks won 73-70 at the 69th Regiment Armory on February 6, and the two teams met in Philadelphia on February 8 in a 20-point blowout win for Ray Lumpp and the Knicks.

On March 5, the teams participated in a doubleheader at the Boston Garden, preceding a game between the Bucks and Celtics later that night.

In 1952-53, when the Knicks went 10-0 against the Bullets en route to a Finals appearance, they played one game in Philly, two games in Boston (one of which went to triple overtime), and even played in Trenton, New Jersey, on March 5, 1953.

Finally, the Bullets snapped the skid on November 14, 1953, behind 19 points by Max Zaslofsky in Baltimore.

Just for the hell of it, here’s some other weird neutral site locations from the 1950s:

January 29, 1952, in Louisville (vs. Indianapolis Olympians)

February 3, 1953, in Buffalo (vs. Milwaukee Hawks)

February 18, 1953, in Providence (vs. Boston Celtics)

January 22, 1954, in New Haven, CT (vs. Philadelphia Warriors)

Several times in 1954-55 in Miami (vs. Fort Wayne Pistons)

November 18, 1954, in Syracuse (vs. Philadelphia Warriors)

March 3, 1955, in Saratoga Springs (vs. Milwaukee Hawks)

March 13, 1956, in Moorhead, MN (vs. Minneapolis Lakers)

January 17, 1957, in Lacrosse, WI (vs. Minneapolis Lakers)

January 14, 1958, in St. Louis (vs. Cincinnati Royals)

February 21, 1958, in Camden, NJ (vs. Philadelphia Warriors)

January 22, 1962, in Moline, IL (vs. Chicago Packers)

March 12, 1962, in Seattle (vs. Los Angeles Lakers)

Various times in Hershey, PA (including the Wilt 100 game)

Pistons, 16 games (2020-24)

We’ve seen a new standard of excellence for the Knicks since the turn of the decade, They have three of these streaks in the last six years!

Back when the Pistons weren’t the annoying playoff contenders we know them as now, they were pretty damn awful. For years, it was a running joke that the COVID-19 pandemic was younger than the last Pistons win over the Knicks.

The streak began on February 8, 2020, when the Knicks overcame an early double-digit deficit to outlast the Pistons in Detroit in a battle of two lowly teams that wouldn’t even be invited to the bubble. Another win on March 8 would mark the team’s final home game with fans for another year due to the pandemic.

As the Knicks ascended, the Pistons stayed bad. On April 4, 2021, the Knicks eviscerated them by a 125-81 margin, the second-biggest blowout in the over 430 games in this matchup.

Even as the meltdown in 2021-22 ensued, the orange and blue survived a scare that March when Marvin Bagley III dropped 27, only for Alec Burks to strip Cade Cunningham in the final seconds to hold on.

The most memorable game of the streak came at the end. Facing the 8-48 Pistons at home in late February, the Knicks came out sleepy and watched as Cunningham nearly dragged his hapless team to the finish line to end the skid at 14, but shenanigans ensued with Donte DiVincenzo to somehow pull it off with a Josh Hart and-1.

Was it a foul? Does anyone really care?

The streak ended on December 7, 2024. We didn’t know it at the time, but the Pistons had finally emerged as threats, and they’d start their own six-game regular-season winning streak against the Knicks that lasted until three weeks ago.

Raptors and Nets, 15 games (active)

The last time the Raptors beat the Knicks? January 22, 2023.

The last time the Nets beat the Knicks? January 28, 2023.

The next opportunity for both to beat the Knicks? Brooklyn gets another chance on December 27, while Toronto next gets a crack on January 20. It’ll be basically four years for both since their last win.

These two streaks are tied for the fourth-longest active streaks in the NBA.

The three longer? OKC over Memphis, Cleveland over Washington, and the Clippers over the Hornets, all at 17. If you thought four years was a lot, it’s been almost 10 since the Hornets beat the Clippers!

These two streaks are very different, but also the same. Both teams have been worse than the Knicks this entire time, sometimes considerably worse, and have yielded some ugly blowouts.

There have also been plenty of scares. There’s the Brunson game-winner in the NBA Cup, the KAT heroics in The Six, the times that Brooklyn puts up a fight but folds late at Barclays Center, and the multiple double-digit comebacks we saw this week.

Either way, those are two Atlantic Division rivals that can’t beat the Knicks. It also comes directly after both dominated the Knicks for prolonged periods.

Remember Nic Claxton’s comments? Well, at the time, the Knicks were 0-9 against the Nets from 2020-23.

The Raptors went a blistering 23-5 against the Knicks from January 2016 to November 2023.

Ain’t no fun when the rabbit’s got the gun.

title: Hegseth uses Venezuela visit to boast of Maduro’s capture by US military
author: Tom Phillips Latin America correspondent
text:
Defense secretary asserts US dominance on trip that would have seemed ‘impossible, almost unbelievable’ a year ago

Pete Hegseth has used his first visit to Venezuela since US special forces abducted its former president, Nicolás Maduro , to boast of the dictator’s capture during what he called “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America”.

Maduro was controversially seized by Delta Force operatives in the early hours of 3 January, setting in motion an improbable rapprochement between Washington and Venezuela’s anti-imperialist “Chavista” regime, which has ruled since 1999.

Speaking outside the recently reopened US embassy in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Wednesday, Hegseth said: “It’s a great honor to be here as the first United States secretary of war this century to set foot in Venezuela.​ Just one year ago my presence here … would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable.

“In fact, exactly one year ago today … [Maduro] stood on a stage not too far from here and yelled mockingly, ‘Come and get me!’” Hegseth recalled, before adding sarcastically: “Well, we answered that call.

“The reality is that … January 3 is the day that will go down in history as a day of liberation for Venezuela,” Hegseth claimed, although Maduro’s allies continue to hold power with US support.

Earlier in the day, Hegseth was welcomed to the Miraflores Palace by Maduro’s former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez , who became acting president with Donald Trump’s blessing after his abduction.

In the aftermath of the deadly US attack, Hegseth was one of the bluntest Trump administration voices when it came to celebrating the invasion. “Maduro had his chance … he effed around and he found out,” the defense secretary bragged .

Speaking at the palace, Hegseth struck a more conciliatory tone as he vowed to deepen cooperation with Venezuela’s new leaders in brief comments that were broadcast by the state broadcaster VTV.

“I stand here on behalf of President Trump, who sends his greeting and looks forward to the opportunities, not just militarily … but also economically: the incredible resource capabilities that your country has, that we look forward to unlocking together with you,” Hegseth told Rodríguez and senior cabinet members, including the defense and foreign ministers, Gustavo González López and Oliver Blanco.

Hegseth said his visit to Rodríguez’s “beautiful country” was designed to re-establish and increase “defense cooperation” between “two great militaries” that less than a year ago were briefly at war. Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that Trump officials were trying to negotiate a long-term US troop presence in Venezuela as part of their push for regional hegemony.

“I appreciate your leadership and commitment to your country,” Hegseth told Maduro’s successor, a once outspoken anti-imperialist leftist who has overseen an unlikely realignment with Washington since her ally was grabbed.

During her five-minute address, Rodríguez, whose oil-rich country is widely seen to have become a US protectorate after January’s invasion, made no mention of Maduro, who is behind bars in New York City.

But referring indirectly to his capture and the subsequent reconciliation with Washington, she told Hegseth: “Thanks to the political and geopolitical maturity of our governments, we have – in a very short period of time, just a few months – turned what were very difficult and very tough times for our people, into an extraordinary space for cooperation and mutual benefit.”

Rodríguez hailed the “historic” energy deal her government recently struck with Trump, who has called it “the biggest oil deal in world history” as well as “the spoils” of his “conquest” of Venezuela.

Hegseth claimed the agreement, which reportedly involves 65bn barrels of reserves, “makes the strait of Hormuz a non-factor for the western hemisphere”.

Critics of Rodríguez’s political movement painted Hegseth’s visit as a humiliating act of genuflection for a president with no choice but to roll out the red carpet for the man whose troops captured her boss.

Writing on X, Luz Mely Reyes, a prominent Venezuelan journalist, said Hegseth’s visit was designed to underscore Washington’s “direct administration” of her country.

“Ten months after Nicolás Maduro’s capture, Washington no longer needs to fire shots to remind everyone who is in charge: the mere presence on Venezuelan soil of the architect of the January incursion reaffirms that the country’s operational sovereignty is subject to the White House’s directives,” Reyes said.

Reyes suspected the visit also carried a message for members of Venezuela’s armed forces. “Domestically, the trip forces the military high command to legitimize the man who directed the extraction of their former commander in chief,” she said. “In this regard, I wonder whether it might be a message of discipline intended to prevent any pockets of resistance in the barracks.”

Trump’s attempts to expand his Shield of the Americas anti-cartel coalition of Latin American governments suffered a major blow last month with the defeat of his far-right ally, Flávio Bolsonaro, in Brazil’s presidential election. The leftwing winner, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has indicated his country will not join the initiative.

But Venezuela’s interim government is in little position to resist. During his surprise visit to Venezuela, Hegseth said Venezuela had gone from being “our most aggressive regional threat to [being] a compliant security partner”. He praised Rodríguez for working “closely, pragmatically, and diligently with the United States to stabilize Venezuela”. Hegseth claimed US and Venezuelan armed forces would work together to attack “narco-terrorists” operating on Venezuelan soil, vowing: “We will hunt you down. We will find you. And we will kill you.”…

title: 24 teams come together to form Collective Cycling Group, the latest venture aiming to 'unlock the value' of pro cycling
author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
text:
Following the collapse of the One Cycling project that aimed to reform professional cycling into a more lucrative business model, a new group has officially made its presence known with similar aims but stronger support. The Collective Cycling Group (CCG) issued a press release on Wednesday announcing the new movement.

It was stated that 24 teams from the men’s and women’s WorldTour and ProTeam ranks have already signed up, and that there are ongoing discussions with additional teams. Several teams have shared news of the announcement, indicating that they are part of the movement, but not all have.

The CCG aims to "develop and market selected commercial rights and activities to strengthen the economic model of professional cycling", according to the announcement.

It also wants to "unlock the value potential of professional cycling, elevate the product to better serve a global fan base, and address the need for a more sustainable economic model in professional road cycling and the broadening of its global reach".

The company is registered in the UK and is essentially the same entity as One Cycling, with government files showing the name was changed to Collective Cycling Group on June 2, 2026.

Soon after, ownership of the project changed hands, with Visma-Lease a Bike team boss Richard Plugge standing down both as a 'director' and 'a person with significant control', and replaced in both cases by Oliver Ciesla, a sports marketing executive who previously worked in motorsport.

"This broad and inclusive initiative by so many teams represents a significant milestone in the long and proud history of the sport," Ciesla said.

"Teams carry much of the sporting and financial risk in professional cycling, while many of the sport’s commercial opportunities remain fragmented. The UCI reform process creates a first opportunity to address these challenges together.

"Through a closer cooperation with organisers, the UCI and other stakeholders, teams can create products that none could offer alone, enhancing the experience of fans worldwide, increasing the sport’s visibility, and contributing to a sustainable economic model."

It was not stated in the launch announcement which 24 teams have signed up to form the Collective Cycling Group.

Some teams have since publicly shared the announcement, indicating they are on board. Those teams include EF Education, which has men’s and women’s WorldTour squads, Canyon-SRAM, and Pinarello-Q36.5.

Given Richard Plugge’s prominent role in One Cycling and the push for reform more generally, it can reasonably be assumed that Visma-Lease a Bike are part of the project.

According to , 13 of the 18 men’s WorldTour teams have signed up. The five absentees were said to be UAE Team Emirates-XRG, Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, Netcompany-Ineos, Jayco-AlUla, and Groupama-FDJ United.

Revamping pro cycling's business model has been a decades-long ambition for many of the stakeholders of a sport

Tour de France owners Amaury Sport Organisation (ASO) are one of the few to be profiting off the sport.

The UCI's formation of the ProTour (now WorldTour) under Hein Verbruggen could be considered to be one of the first attempts at modernizing pro cycling, although the effort was met with extreme resistance from the ASO.

The WorldTour promised to bring more stability to teams, with three-year guaranteed entry into the biggest races, but the sponsorship model of professional cycling remains on shaky ground.

Teams with billionaire backers and generous budgets dominate the sport, while smaller outfits such as TotalEnergies have had to fight for their lives after sponsors pull out.

Even One Cycling wasn't the first try at a new model: In 2011, the Rothschild financial group were backers of what was then called a 'breakaway league' - the World Series Cycling (WSC), with 14 teams on board.

The Velon group came in 2014, with a more modest ambition to add on-board footage and real-time rider stats to their marketing campaigns. How teams really benefited from being a part of Velon is less concrete, and mainly helps with fan engagement and commercialization.

How the CCG will differ from the previous attempts remain to be seen.

How the new CCG project will be received by the UCI should become more clear after the WorldTour seminar, which runs from December 9-10, 2026.

The topics included calendar and participation, the economic model, fan engagement, safety and integrity.

Some of the ideas floated in the document include shortening Grand Tours to 16 days, budget caps, and joint broadcast rights.

‘An honour’: Pochettino up for challenge of leading Manchester United revival
author: Will Unwin
text:
New head coach faces tough opening match at Anfield

‘It’s a big challenge but at the same time it’s adrenaline’

Mauricio Pochettino said it was “an honour” and “a privilege” to be the new Manchester United head coach after arriving in England on Wednesday.

Pochettino flew from Cincinnati to Manchester overnight after overseeing the USA beating Haiti in his final game in charge. Members of Pochettino’s staff landed earlier in the week to begin work at Carrington , laying the foundations as United seek to turn their season around. His right-hand man, Jesús Pérez, the goalkeeping coach Toni Jiménez and the fitness coach Sebastiano Pochettino, who continues to work with his father, have already taken training with those not on international duty.

Those away with their national teams will return to the club on Thursday, when they are expected to meet Pochettino for the first time and hold meetings. Conversations have also been held with various departments within the club, as Pochettino sought to learn about the squad’s health as he seeks areas of improvement.

Pochettino’s first challenge will be at Anfield on Sunday, when 18th-placed United take on Liverpool. The 54-year-old has his eyes set on rattling Manchester City after being told on TNT Sports that “Manchester’s blue and always will be blue” by DaMarcus Beasley, who once had a loan spell with City. Pochettino responded: “No way. You will see. Give me time … give me time and that is going to start to change.”

Speaking about joining United, Pochettino said: “It’s a big challenge but at the same time, it’s adrenaline that you want to feel because I think we are going to have a different job. But I think one of the things that is important is that we have the experience to deal with that, and I think we need to add our common sense and the way we are going to approach all the things.

“We know that the situation is not a situation that a club like Manchester United deserves,” Pochettino added. “The fanbase is amazing and after we signed here in America, of every 10 people I crossed in the street, nine are Manchester United fans. It’s amazing.”

Pochettino is also reunited with the strength and conditioning coach Silvia Tuya, the analyst Alec Scott and his long-term assistant, Miki D’Agostino, at Old Trafford.

title: 24 Top Cycling Teams Are Making A New Money Move To Fix Cycling’s Business Model
author: ahood
text:
Teams are floating a new project to collectively sell what they bring to the peloton. (Photo: Loic VENANCE / AFP via Getty Images)

Top pro teams are taking another stab at trying to fix cycling’s business model.

Some 24 squads are forming a company designed to turn their collective commercial muscle into new revenue steams.

Collective Cycling Group Ltd. (CCG), a UK-based business owned by participating teams, announced a shareholder agreement including teams from the men’s and women’s WorldTour and ProTeam ranks.

Discussions with additional teams are ongoing, a statement confirmed Wednesday.

“Teams carry much of the sporting and financial risk in professional cycling, while many of the sport’s commercial opportunities remain fragmented,” CCG director Oliver Ciesla said in the announcement. “The UCI reform process creates a first opportunity to address these challenges together.”

Instead of making a run directly at TV rights, which are controlled by races, teams are looking at what they bring to the table in the form of cycling’s biggest stars.

The idea is to bundle what they have into something bigger that fans, broadcasters, and sponsors might be interested in paying money for.

That includes team commercial rights, data, media content, merchandising, hospitality, and fan experiences.

The end game is to give teams a stronger financial footing rather than leaving them constantly chasing the next sponsor and relying almost exclusively on sponsorship backing to underwrite ever-rising team budgets.

The announcement follows the stalled ONE Cycling project , which died on the vine after the UCI rejected it in June 2025 .

Corporate filings show CCG previously operated under the name OneCycling Limited, according to Reuters .

The release doesn’t mention a new racing series or a call for shared broadcast revenues.

Instead, the focus is on developing commercial opportunities around assets the teams already hold.

They hope to organize their newest project as part of the UCI’s ongoing Project 2030 effort to reshape professional road cycling.

The announcement does not identify the 24 teams, disclose financial commitments, or set a timetable for its first products.

Cycling’s tried this before. Let’s see if something will change.

title: Testing the Tech and Heat Training Required to Survive a 95-Degree Tour de France
author: Will Tracy
text:
There is a giant vault in Bolzano, Italy that can simulate elevation higher than Mount Everest, a freeze as cold as Siberia, and temperatures so hot that they are used to help train firefighters. On October 21, I stepped into that vault wearing nothing but a cycling kit and shoes.

As I swung my leg over a stationary bike, the fans revved up in front of me as the chamber adjusted its climate to match Stage 2 of this year’s Tour de France. It was a hot day in Barcelona when Isaac del Toro won ahead of Tadej Pogacar and Remco Evenepoel. By the end of the Tour, it was the hottest race on record with an average temperature of 32.4°C (90.3°F) across the 21 stages.

Excessive heat usually means a decline in performance. But with the advent of heat training, cooling strategies, and ever-improving clothing technology, professional cyclists are faster than ever, even during the hottest Tour de France in history.

The moment I stepped into the vault — the TerraX Cube — I knew what was at stake. I was here alongside the CORE team and more than 20 other journalists to test the new Q36.5 Gregarius Pro Evo Jersey, Base Layer Subzero, and Dottore Pro Bib Shorts. The vault was set to 35°C (95°F) degrees with a humidity of 50%, far from the ideal temperature to achieve peak performance. I had just done a heat training session in CORE’s Sweatlab, so I had a baseline of data for what I could expect as my core temperature rose.

Not only were we going to ride in excessive heat, we were going to simulate the finale of Stage 2 of the Tour using a custom workout on Zwift. Here was the workout , along with my power targets based on my FTP:

I was already dripping sweat during the warmup thanks to the ambient temperature, and my sweat rate intensified as my power increased to 360w. After a quick recovery, we began the hardest part of the test (in my opinion): four minutes at VO2 Max in 95-degree heat. This is the type of effort short enough that you can maintain an output above threshold, but long enough that your heart rate and RPE will be jacked up by the end of the effort.

The final few intervals went by fast as I could see the metaphorical finish line in front of me. And just like that, it was all over. CORE gathered data from our body temperature sensors, and we shuffled our way into the cool hallway. The testing was over; now it was time to look at the results.

To my surprise, our performances in the heat chamber didn’t drop off significantly. In fact, many riders (myself included) performed at their best despite the hot conditions. This was a sharp contrast to my data from CORE’s Sweatlab where I pushed myself to the limit without ever breaking 300w.

The lab test at CORE – done two days before the test in Bolzano – was a data-gathering mission. I wasn’t there to chase power PBs or set an impressive time. I was there to sweat; and that I did.

During the normal cooling conditions, I wore a cycling kit and had two fans pointed towards me. I was riding on a Zwift Ride with ERG mode turned on, so my power output was steady to the Watt. The initial 15-minute interval established the baseline where my heart rate was steady at 138 bpm, and my core temperature stabilized at 38°C (100.4°F).

The hard part was up next: 35 minutes of heat training. That meant pulling on the CORE heat training suit, turning the fans off, and turning the heater on. Within minutes, my sweat started pooling on the floor. Over the course of 35 minutes, my heart rate rose from 138 bpm to 175 bpm without any change in power. I rode at 280w the entire time, but it felt like I was doing a threshold interval for the last 15 minutes.

That is the damage that heat can do to your performance. Without sufficient cooling, Zone 2 power can feel like Zone 4 power once your heat strain reaches a certain level. That was the kind of performance degradation that CORE was looking for in the Italian climate cube. But the closer they looked at the results, the more they realized that the clothing had worked.

We were all wearing Q36.5 kit in the climate chamber, specifically designed for use in 30°C+ (86°F) heat. Tom Pidcock loves heat training, and it was no surprise to hear that he plays a major role in the R&D of Q36.5 kit. (Fun fact: he’s also the only rider on Pinarello Q36.5 Pro Cycling Team who wears an XXS skinsuit.)

As I pored through my own performance data, I remembered how good my legs felt during the final two-minute interval in the heat chamber. Despite feeling hot, my body had performed extremely well in the conditions. Personally, that is the biggest difference that I’ve noticed after doing a heat training block.

Without heat acclimatization, my body has typically reacted to the heat like it did in CORE’s Sweatlab. My heart rate would rise uncontrollably as my legs are drained of their strength. But after a big heat training block, I noticed that I could still hit my best power numbers in excessively hot conditions. Not only would my heart rate be 10 bpm lower than expected, but it would stabilize during long efforts in the heat – quite the opposite of what I experienced in the CORE Sweatlab.

One of my biggest takeaways was that the clothing had worked. This wasn’t the only heat adaptation method that I asked Q36.5 and CORE about during this trip. I also asked about cold drinks, pouring water over your head, rubbing ice cubes on your wrists, and of course, heat training. Let’s start with what does work.

Cold drinks and gels are probably the most effective ways to cool your body from the inside out. When you’re talking about performance degradation in the heat, you are most often talking about an increase in core temperature as well as an increase in skin temperature. This is known as heat strain, something that CORE quantifies with their sensor and app, and the key metric that many riders use for heat training.…

title: Primož Roglič Lands a Contract to Join NSN Cycling for 2027
author: ahood
text:
Roglič joins NSN on a one-year deal. (Photo: Marco BERTORELLO / AFP via Getty Images)

Primož Roglič will race in 2027 and will join NSN Cycling on a one-year deal.

In a late-hour move, the deal means the 37-year-old Slovenian will be in the WorldTour peloton next season.

“I always like challenges,” Roglič said in a team note. “That’s why I’m here, to take these on together and see what the future brings us.

“It took me some time to figure out how to make a chapter in my life where I am peaceful, but the answer is actually simple with the team name: Never Say Never. It feels like the perfect connection.”

Roglič, one of the superstars over the past decade, was looking down the barrel at possible retirement at the end of 2026.

Talks with several teams ended without a signature , but things came together quickly with NSN Cycling.

“From the first moment we spoke, it was evident that Primož still has a lot of passion for the sport and a drive to be the best he can,” said NSN Cycling general manager Kjell Carlström. “It was an easy decision to make.”

The former ski jumper ended his three-year run with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe after a season that included second overall at the Vuelta a España and a win at the European time trial championship.

It was more of a question if he wanted to keep racing and at what price.

Roglič was sometimes bizarrely ambivalent in his public statements about his future, but he was talking with several teams behind the scenes.

Talks petered out, however, with one team after another. NSN offered a one-year contract but no financial details were revealed.

Roglič was reportedly earning around $3 million a year with Red Bull, so a high asking price might have been a factor on some teams taking a pass on the veteran.

Roglič — a winner of five grand tours — will link up with Richard Carapaz, Santiago Buitrago, and Lennert Van Eetvelt on the reinvigorated NSN lineup.

“This signing reflects the ambition we have for the future. We want to compete at the highest level, challenge for major results and continue building a team capable of achieving great things,” Carlström said. “We are confident that Primož can play an important role in that journey, and we look forward to seeing him race in NSN colors.”

Roglič scored nearly 1,000 UCI points in 2026 , something that will come in handy if he can repeat it next season for NSN Cycling.

The team — formerly Israel-Premier Tech — finished ranked 19th in the rolling three-year WorldTour rankings, one spot out of the guaranteed top 18 licenses.

There’s no news yet on a possible calendar, but at NSN he should see plenty of chances to race.

“I still believe I have some work to do, in both racing and with myself,” Roglič said. “I have the drive and also the attitude not just to race, but also achieve things.”

The team broke the news on social media, with a smiling Roglič using a “like and follow” of the team’s social media channel.

Roglič — who was beaten by Tadej Pogačar at the wild TT finale at the 2020 Tour de France — will join his new teammates at a winter camp in Spain next month.

title: Primož Roglič will continue racing into 2027 as new team for 'final chapter' is finally revealed
author: James Moultrie
text:
After months of speculation, Primož Roglič will continue his career into 2027, having signed with NSN Cycling Team on a one-year contract.

The 37-year-old looked to be heading for retirement after his time with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe came to an end – despite being the reigning European time trial champion and having finished second at the Vuelta a España in September – but with NSN, he has found a place for the final chapter of his storied career.

A five-time Grand Tour winner, Roglič will make up part of the Swiss WorldTour team’s general classification ambitions, alongside fellow new signings for 2027, Richard Carapaz and Lennert Van Eetvelt.

"I always like challenges. That's why I'm here, to take these on together and see what the future brings us," said Roglič on the team's website.

"It took me some time to figure out how to make a chapter in my life where I am peaceful, but the answer is actually simple with the team name: Never Say Never. It feels like the perfect connection.

"I still believe I have some work to do – in both racing and with myself. I have the drive and also the attitude not just to race, but also achieve things."

10 years after his first WorldTour season with LottoNL-Jumbo, former ski jumper Roglič will arrive at NSN as the rider with the most victories among active men's pros at 93, only trailing Slovenian compatriot Tadej Pogačar.

Now into his late 30s, he's raced limited calendars in recent seasons, but can still ramp up his performance for the big occasion at Grand Tours, finishing second at the most recent Vuelta, eighth at last year's Tour de France, and winning his fourth Vuelta title as recently as 2024.

Delighted by bringing in the talents of one of the modern era's best GC riders, NSN revealed their new star signing with a social media post of Roglič following NSN on Instagram.

"Welcoming Primož Roglič to NSN Cycling Team is a hugely exciting moment for our organization. From the first moment we spoke, it was evident that Primož still has a lot of passion for the sport and a drive to be the best he can. It was an easy decision to make," said NSN General Manager Kjell Carlström.

"Primož is one of the outstanding riders of his generation. His achievements speak for themselves, and the opportunity to bring someone with his experience, quality and winning mentality into our team is something we are incredibly proud of.

"This signing reflects the ambition we have for the future. We want to compete at the highest level, challenge for major results and continue building a team capable of achieving great things. We are confident that Primož can play an important role in that journey, and we look forward to seeing him race in NSN colours."

Mauricio Pochettino’s USMNT time will be remembered fondly, but it wasn’t transformational
author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
text:
The incoming Manchester United manager improved the US team’s culture and competitiveness, but could not bring about sea change in two years

I n a theater high up in a midtown Manhattan skyscraper built from lots of glass, a highlight reel played to deafening music. And then, on “a monumental day for US Soccer”, federation president, Cindy Parlow Cone, announced they had bagged their man, Mauricio Pochettino , to become the highest-profile United States manager in the men’s national team’s history.

Pochettino held court for three-quarters of an hour in his signature blend of Spanglish before the assembled media and a grab bag of sponsors. Then he recorded some TV hits. And after that, in a bit of accidental prescience, he went off to record a podcast with Gary Neville.

Two years, two months, and a week later, he presided over the USMNT’s untroubled 2-0 win over Haiti in Cincinnati on Tuesday, putting a bow on an 8-0 aggregate victory in the Concacaf Nations League quarter-finals. He did a lot of hugging afterwards, a staple of what was briefly mooted as Pochismo . He posed for a group picture with federation staffers. There were tears in the locker room.

After a 6-0 romp in the first leg on Saturday, Pochettino left his starting XI unchanged, raising some eyebrows. Perhaps he hoped to leave with another emphatic result; maybe he was buffing up his final stats in charge of the USA; or possibly he was legitimately concerned about giving away a lead of half a dozen goals.

It will probably be the last time in quite a long while that Pochettino enjoys a pair of consecutive lopsided victories. He boarded a private jet after the game to take over Manchester United just as soon it landed in England in the morning, leaving a situation where he enjoyed a bank vault’s worth of credit for one where his every result will be dissected and scrutinized for his viability in the job.

For all the hype, for the $6m annual salary – about double what the previous record earner at the federation, Jürgen Klinsmann, had made – and for all the talk of belief and culture and fight, what did Pochettino actually leave behind for his successor to build on? He was impactful, certainly, turning around a moody and slumping generation ambling into a home World Cup bereft of momentum or much discernible enthusiasm. The Argentinian roused the ballyhooed golden generation for four-fifths of a very strong World Cup, turning in displays more convincing and dominant than the program has ever managed on that stage – until it all came undone against Belgium in the last 16.

His time in charge was notable, absolutely. Pochettino got, and brought, lots of attention to the team, although it’s hard to say whether a more workaday manager might not have ridden that same World Cup wave, as the voice of the co-hosts.

Pochettino wasn’t the first USMNT manager to try to play more expansively, more technically, in a more aesthetically pleasing way. Klinsmann tried it, and Gregg Berhalter tried it, too. But Klinsmann didn’t have the players, and Berhalter’s weren’t ready for it. Pochettino did and they were, at long last, and he introduced a tactical sophistication, with deft attacking patterns that regularly unlocked useful spaces.

He also wasn’t the first USMNT manager to fixate on culture and give young talent a chance. But through his selections and his messaging, he reinstated an internal competition for playing time that had seeped away under several consecutive and at times complacent administrations. And he deepened the player pool considerably. Perhaps any old head coach would have spotted the glut of gifted teenagers pushing through and had the wherewithal to bring them along, but Pochettino deserves credit for leaning on the young players, handing them meaningful minutes and responsibility.

While Pochettino leaves the USMNT better than he found them, his spell in charge was not transformational. He brought the Americans no further at a World Cup than they had been before. His statistics – victories in 62% of his matches; 2.08 goals scored per game; 1.29 conceded – are more or less in line with the numbers put up by his permanent predecessors. He did not win the Concacaf Gold Cup or the Nations League when he was occasioned to.

Nor did he take the US to their first World Cup in four decades, as Bob Gansler did in 1990. Or make them respectable on that stage, as Bora Milutinovic did in 1994. Or bring about their breakthrough, as Bruce Arena did in 2002. Or rebuild the program from its modern nadir, as Berhalter did in his first tenure. It is a sign of growth, perhaps, that the strides available to be made were smaller. You can only overcome the challenges you are faced with, after all.

Whatever the case, Pochettino will be remembered fondly by most. He smiled and joked a lot and did his best to say interesting things. He could be spiky , from time to time, but mostly injected an environment that had grown stale and dour with joy.

Pochettino, by all accounts, had a good time stateside, commuting here from his homes in London and Barcelona. He enjoyed watching NFL games and attended the Cincinnati Bengals’ home victory over the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday. He got into country music, apparently. “Only we can say thank you,” Pochettino said in his final news conference, on behalf of his staff. “Thank you so much, and always we are going to keep the good memories.”

The USMNT, too, largely enjoyed their time with their famous coach. They made some nice memories together. But he may not have been here long enough to fundamentally change their trajectory.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now . He teaches at Marist University.

title: Broken frame no problem for Lukas Malezsewski, who wins UCI Gravel race after being hit by a driver
author: Owen Rogers
text:
A broken chainstay proved no problem for Belgian gravel racer Lukas Malezsewski, who won the Greek round of the UCI Gravel World Series last weekend.

Riding for Greg van Avermaet’s GVA Gold team, Malezsewski was just 17km into The Gravel of Marathon race when the incident happened: a driver hit him, breaking the chainstay on the drive side of his Basso bike frame.

But rather than give up, the 25-year-old remounted and raced on, eventually winning the Elite Men’s race more than three minutes ahead of second-placed Kasper Enstad.

In its first edition, The Gravel of Marathon is the first UCI round of the UCI Gravel World Series to be staged in Greece, starting and finishing in the ancient city of Marathon. The Elite men raced over a 95km course, which, though relatively short, comprised more than 1,300m of vertical ascent, with 71% of the course off-road.

Malezsewski was hit by the vehicle after the day’s first climb, and not long after emerging from the route’s second gravel sector. "Got hit by a car after 17km and broke my frame. Still made it to the finish line in first place," Malezsewski wrote in an Instagram post.

Rather than treading the well-worn path to gravel from road racing, Malezsewski is an accomplished mountain bike rider, winning the European junior title in 2019 and the Belgian under-23 title in 2022, though he’s not raced at UCI level since 2024.

While he’s raced occasionally at national and UCI .2 level on the road since then, he’s concentrated on gravel.

And to great effect, winning two UCI races last year and repeating the feat this season, when he won Tartu Rattmaraton in Estonia in mid-September, before finishing in the top six of every other race he started before last weekend’s Greek event.

title: 'Tour de France Femmes goal for 2029' – There’s a new US team on the scene, and they have big ambitions
author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
text:
The paperwork has been submitted to the UCI and Dr. Andrea Cyr expects to lead the next US-based Continental women's team, Orange Seal presented by Autowurks, in 2027.

The team will be based in Austin, Texas with a "clear ambition" to become a top-25 team in the world with a majority of riders from the United States, and to earn a place in the Tour de France Femmes by 2029.

"We have high aspirations, but the first step is we're going to be a Continental team for 2027. We want to be a ProTeam in 2028, that's where you start to get a lot of the invites like the Classics and bigger UCI stage racing. Then we have a Tour to France Femmes goal of 2029," Cyr told .

"A lot of this is sparked by my own ambition too. There's some development programmes to get people interested in the sport and then there's WorldTour, but there's nothing in between. I'm in a unique position, with resources and networking to actually put things together. A year ago this was not the plan."

The new team merges Cyr's HigherDOSE-Renova criterium-based programme with the former ROXO Continental women's squad, which last competed in 2024 as Boneshaker Project presented by Orange Seal.

"We didn't want this to just be a one-year adventure. We wanted to do something a little bit more sustainable," Cyr said about the next step after HigherDOSE. "So we started conversations with a management group from Texas. All three of these guys have different roles, they've known each other for like 20 years. I think they have found new vigor and motivation through this too."

Leadership at Orange Seal p/b Autowurks includes former WorldTour rider Chann McRae as head sports director, Austin attorney Todd Reed as team manager, and real estate executive Charlie Tames as co-owner. The trio had most recently been involved in supporting French women's ProTeam Mayenne Monbana My Pie. Justin Kirk will split time as a sports director with the women's team and the Texas Roadhouse elite masters team. This quartet of management, along with Cyr, form the ownership group for the team.

"Our goal is to build a top-25 team in the world with a majority of riders from the United States and the resources to compete in the biggest races. Bringing these programs together gives us an established foundation to build on," Tames said in a team statement after a formal launch party in Austin on November 15.

"The 2027 season is the first step toward our top-25 ambition and our goal of reaching the Tour de France Femmes by 2029."

More than half of the roster will come from HigherDOSE, including Cyr and Seitz, with Marjie Bemis, Elizabeth Dixon and Odette Lynch preserving the foundation created in 2026. The ROXO connection brings Femenina a Guatemala stage winner Kira Payer, as well as additional leadership and resources to support the next stage of growth.

Other new riders include Canadian Jenna Nestman, former Fount Cycling rider Alia Shafi, and Nicole Steinmetz, who previously raced for Cynisca and Virginia's Blue Ridge TWENTY24. According to Cyr, two more riders have been offered contracts and the full roster will be confirmed in the coming weeks.

"American racers are struggling, and it's really struggling on the women's side. I personally started shifting my own goals and my own thinking, and I had a really good result at Pro Road Nationals, a top 10 in the road race, fourth in the crit, and then had a really good result at Philly. I got to thinking, maybe I'm more than just a crit racer," Cyr described to her inspiration to form a new team.

"It was really awesome to have Philly back, and I finished that race [top 15 - Ed.], and I was like, 'That was the best day ever! Like that was my favorite ever.'

"We need more of this, like hard racing with strong teams and strong riders from all over the world. This is what I'm craving, and I know I'm not alone in that. I know a lot of other female racers are probably looking for the same thing."

Once Continental status is confirmed, the team plans to firm the 2027 calendar with UCI races in South America and Europe for the spring, and a return block of racing to Europe in July and August. Key US races will include Redlands Bicycle Classic, Tour of the Gila, USPro Road Nationals and Philadelphia Cycling Classic p/b AmeriGas, as well as a selection of criteriums.

"We want a well-rounded race calendar, but also aware of our short and long-term goals. To achieve our long-term goals, we need to get points and really establish quickly as a strong, confident team," Cyr said.

"It's important to stay engaged with the racing we have here in the U.S., which is a lot of criterium racing. It's good for sponsors."

Orange Seal joins as title sponsor, with Autowurks as presenting sponsor. The team is also supported by bike sponsor Winspace with equipment and apparel partners ABUS, Tifosi, MUMU and Schwalbe.
