title: Netcompany Ineos lose significant sponsor as TotalEnergies confirms it will not continue in 2027
author: Patrick Fletcher
text:
With TotalEnergies moving its financial resources away from the eponymous French ProTeam – which will become XEFI in 2027 – and over to one of the leading women's teams, there were question marks over the company's relationship with the Ineos team.

And now a spokesperson has confirmed to that the sponsorship will not continue beyond this season.

"At the conclusion of these two seasons of sponsorship, TotalEnergies would like to thank the Netcompany INEOS team for its commitment and professionalism, as well as all of its riders, who kept us inspired and excited through their sporting achivements," read a statement.

The news will raise new questions over the finances of Netcompany Ineos, especially in light of the ongoing reports of financial headaches at Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos empire, and the general move towards dilution of its sporting projects.

The company gave up its sole title sponsor’s slot at the cycling team this year, as the Danish IT firm Netcompany was welcomed as a major new backer on a five-year deal.

However, Netcompany’s arrival was not the end of the story, with Tom Hill, the team’s chief commercial officer, saying soon after: “We’re going back to market looking for a second co-title partner.”

There were widespread reports since its arrival at the team in 2025 that TotalEnergies were exploring options for escalation of its sponsorship, including here on where we reported earlier this year that co-title sponsorship was under discussion.

The French energy giant had been clear that it would end its 10-year title backing of Jean-René Bernaudeau’s French team at the end of this season, but clearly wanted to stay in cycling elsewhere.

However, the idea of furthering of the Ineos partnership has broken down at some point and the energy company has gone down a different road, throwing its weight into women’s cycling and the French team that’s home to the world’s top rider, Demi Vollering.

It was interesting that the FDJ team’s manager, Stephen Delcourt, told Cyclingnews that the deal with TotalEnergies came together “very, very fast”, with contact first initiated around the Tour de France Femmes and tied up in a ground-breaking five year deal only a matter of weeks afterwards.

Today’s statement confirms that all its eggs are now in that basket, which raises interesting questions surrounding value for money in terms of the amounts required for the various sponsorship tiers comparing men’s and women’s cycling.

As for Netcompany Ineos, there are no serious doubts surrounding their future after Netcompany’s long-term commitment earlier this year, but the breakdown in the TotalEnergies relationship raises question marks, over how the team will reach the sort of funding levels that the team themselves have acknowledged are required to return to super-team status.

title: Hunt Limitless 40 Gravel Aero wheelset review: Good to a fault
author: andy@atpperformance.uk (Andy Turner)
text:
£1,479.00 / $1,849 / €1,849

1431g claimed,1478g measured with lock rings and tape

40mm front 41mm rear

36mm ext 27mm int Front, 35mm ext 26mm int Rear

With this wheelset, Hunt has applied its Limitless aero technology from the road to gravel, and given my impressions from riding them, it has achieved its goal of making a highly versatile gravel race wheelset to match the latest gravel race frames .

The weight is competitive against some of the best at this depth, making it an impressively good value wheelset. So much so, in fact, that I see no good reason to go for the UD spoke and Ceramic Speed bearing upgrade of this wheelset for another £1000.

But there is the question of tyre width optimisation. Gravel is fast evolving, but current trends are towards wider and wider tyre offerings, with 50mm+ being common across modern races and frame design. These rims are perfect for 40-45mm offerings, but perhaps missing out when it comes to fitting the larger widths that are more prevalent now across races and adventure riding.

Hunt has since released its 5AM Gravel wheelset to cater to that market. They recently tested very well in our wind tunnel gravel wheel shootout , and a review of those will follow in due course.

Design and specifications

These wheels have been designed for racing; At launch, Hunt explicitly stated that this rim shape was designed to be its fastest and most versatile gravel wheelset.

This was done via a combination of CFD (computational fluid dynamics) and wind tunnel development, but also with rider input from sponsored racers. The argument was that modern gravel racing is now mirroring the speed and tactics of road racing. I’d argue that given the speeds of the two, and tactics are very race dependent, but there’s no doubt gravel racing is faster every year.

These Limitless 40 rims have been specifically designed to be optimised with the 40 and 45mm Schwalbe G-One gravel tyres. Testing, which is published on the Hunt website, shows that the Limitless 40 rims were fastest bar the 3T Dicuss 45/50, but those came in at over 300g heavier.

The reason for differing rim profile was due to finding that the air interacts differently with the front and rear wheels, and a wider front and narrower rear was optimal for aero and stability. It’s not an uncommon theme in wheels both on the road and off.

Meanwhile this Limitless technology results in a more squared off rim profile, similar to the latest Roval Terra CLX Aero wheels. This aims to be stable in crosswinds, lighter, and result in a longer virtual aerofoil by cutting the V shape that would be present on a deeper rim, but the idea is that the air continues to flow as if this V is present and elongated, thus ideally resulting in greater aero performance at a shallower depth.

The rim itself is made of unidirectional T24/30 carbon fibre with 3K weave re-enforced spoke holes. Hookless TSS profile is used, with a 4.5mm thick bead to reduce the chance of pinch flats and make the rims stronger in case of a rim strike. Although 40-45mm tyres are recommended, the wheels are safe to use with 35-60mm options.

Spokes are Pillar Wing 20 Elliptical Aero Stainless Steel, with 24 front and rear in a two-cross 1:1 ratio lacing pattern. Dual full-contact sealed cartridge bearings are used with a proprietary waterproof grease used to improve longevity and assist in smooth running across foul weather use. The 48t ratchet drive system at the rear offers fast engagement for accelerations.

Spare spokes are also included with the wheels, along with valves and lockrings, which is not always a given with wheelsets. Proper wheel bags are also included.

First things first, the fitting of tyres. With rims becoming wider and wider, I personally find that tends to mean tyres are more of a pain to fit, with levers being required alongside the elbow grease and trusty grippy gloves. Fitting the Panaracer Gravel King ZX 45mm tyres I’ve been using for all my gravel wheel tests, they were no harder or easier to fit on these rims than similar options.

These are however my first foray into hookless gravel rims. I don’t like hookless for road, mainly because I’m a taller and larger rider, so pressures under 70 PSI feel far too cushioned and squishy for me and make fast cornering unpleasant and the bike feel disconnected.

For gravel, however, this changes. These rims have a max pressure of 58 PSI, which is more than I would use on the tarmac with 45mm tyres, let alone off-road where 30 is around the max pressure I’d run. In this scenario, I am liking hookless quite a lot. It makes leveraging a tyre hook under the bead easy for stubborn removals and promises to reduce manufacturing costs while cutting weight. The super wide rim bead should also be nicely sturdy in the event of a stone strike, but I have not sought those out intentionally.

Weight is an area where these wheels perform pretty well. For the price and depth, 1478g (heavier than claimed but includes lock rings) is fairly lightweight. It’s just over 100g heavier than the UD carbon spoked equipped variant, but that wheelset is the same rim for £1000 more, with ceramic bearings as well. For accelerations I’ve found them responsive, and slow speed climbing does not feel laborious.

Another component that impacts the rapid acceleration is the 48 tooth engagement ratchet. Often these are 36t, which means a 10° engagement, while 48t offers a 7.5° response, so the hub engages after a lesser percentage of the pedal stroke. Some claim that more teeth can reduce longevity, but I’ve yet to have a problem with that.

The rim itself feels nicely stiff, without being excessively so for gravel use. It’s a truncated profile, like the new Roval Terra Aero squared off rim. Spoke lacing wise, the 1:1 two-cross 24 straight pull spoke pattern isn’t anything special on paper, but the wheel feels well balanced without any lag in response when accelerating, while there isn’t any ‘flop’ when banking over.

I have been getting a few spoke pinging noises on rides though, and have yet to be able to determine the cause, but the wheels run true and without issue.

A big component of the performance of this wheelset does depend on what side of the fence you sit on when it comes to tyre widths. I’ve tested everything from 38mm up to 55mm tyres for gravel, and there are pros and cons to each.

We’ve gone through aero testing of gravel tyres , but this metric is very dependent on the rim shape. For example, the new ENVE SES 6.7 Pro G wheelset is incredibly wide, and fast according to our testing, so it can be more aero with wider tyres. Meanwhile the Hunt Limitless rim is narrower, and has been designed specifically for 40-45mm wide tyres.

Personally, I have used 45mm for events like Graean Gravel, and as a rear tyre for Gralloch. It is a good balance of wide enough for most gravel surfaces, while not being as heavy as a 50mm+.

However, over rough gravel a 50mm tyre does feel more cushioned, and results in less fatigue, while also giving exceptional handling on loose corners. This is a trend that has grown in gravel, with 50-60mm options now being common, and with that, a wider rim is required to really maximise performance.

To that end, the Hunt Limitless 40 rim already shows its age, and the newer 5AM Gravel is a good, more modern alternative, but it does come at a £500 uplift.

The Hunt Limitless 40 gravel wheelset is an impressively good value wheelset. For the difference of 100g and lack of carbon spokes, it is £1000 cheaper than the UD Carbon spoke version with the same rim.

I also appreciate that lockrings, spare spokes, valves and wheel bags have been included, as even on higher range offerings these often get left out, and they are not items I think people should need to consider purchasing when getting a wheelset.

There are other good value offerings available, such as the Parcours FKT (£1249) which is a little heavier, but deeper and designed for wider tyres, and the Reserve 40/44 GR (£1599) and Scope R4.G (£1498) which are both very similar on paper.

Given the inclusion of spares, plus the ease of customer service, certainly in the UK, I am a big fan of the Hunt Limitless 40 wheels.

The only downside to me personally is that the rims could do with being a touch wider for the trend towards 50mm and up in tyres. However, for a lot of gravel riding scenarios, either hardpack or tarmac and bike paths, 45mm is perfectly adequate and these rims are well designed to work with those. If you are planning on tackling looser gravel, large stones, and plenty of wet weather events, then you may find better value in a wider rim to accommodate 50mm+ tyres.

The HUNT Limitless 40 gravel wheelset is such an attractive offering that it makes the higher specification Limitless 40 models with carbon spokes and ceramic bearings appear somewhat obsolete due to the better value of these.

The weight is competitive with more expensive offerings, while performance with 45mm tyres is brilliant.

If you're looking for something a little more performance oriented or futureproof, then the newer 5AM Gravel wheels would be a better bet, but for most people, 45mm tyres can still be the go-to for a lot of gravel riding and racing, and these are a solid choice.

These could look a little more exciting, as matte finishes look dirty quickly, but that is the limit of my critique.

I like a solid rim bed personally, but the tyres seat and hold pressure well, while the hookless performance is good as more tyres adhere to the TSS standard.

I haven’t felt lacking with these wheels at any point, there have been some spoke pings at points but the wheels are in perfect working order.

There are some properly lightweight gravel wheel offerings on the market now at a similar depth, but the HUNT are still very much at the competitive end given the depth and the price.

It’s hard to fault the value here with the price, customer care, and where it sits in the competitive rankings. The only downside I can possibly see is if you want the best aero for 50mm+ tyres, but then those offerings are substantially more expensive

title: Tour de France breakaway star heads to Southeast Asia for 2,500km charity solo bike trip – Video
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
The 26-year-old Lotto-Intermarché rider is ending his offseason in an alternative way, embarking on a 2,500km, 19-day trip in Vietnam and Cambodia. He's raising funds for Molembike , a charity in Molenbeek, Brussels, which is dedicated to promoting social cohesion through cycling.

Veistroffer will donate €5,000 to the charity, while sponsors Ekoï and Lotto will each contribute €1 for each kilometre he rides during the adventure.

It's a far cry from the usual winter training activities pro racers usually take on in Spain, which Veistroffer described to as "Training camp in Calpe, climbing the Coll de Rates fifty times, doing the same out-and-back route twenty times. The routine for ten years."

He's travelling light on his trip, heading out on an Orbea Terra gravel bike equipped with three panniers and two sets of kit as well as some changes of clothes for the evenings. "I still have room enough to bring back a few souvenirs," he said.

Veistroffer, who turned pro with Lotto last year and won a stage of the Tour of Oman this spring, will document the trip on his YouTube channel. He's uploaded an episode taking viewers through his route planning, schedule, and gear, and on Monday he uploaded the first episode of his travels in Vietnam.

He's set to take on 19 days of riding, each measuring between 140km and 180km, with his only real requirement to make his return flight to Europe on December 2.

"I don't know yet where I'll stop, but I intend to avoid touristy spots," he said.

"The first third of the journey will be fairly flat, through rice paddies. Then, near the Cambodian border, I'll find a mountainous area, passes at 1,500 meters altitude, a more tropical feel; cocoa and coffee fields, magnificent sunsets. Towards the end, I'll follow the South China Sea."

Veistroffer logged 94 race days and 14,248km this season, the most in the professional peloton, but he's showing no signs of slowing down. His Asian trip has the full backing of his Lotto team, of course.

"It's almost a Grand Tour. It's the first of the 2027 season or the last of 2026; it's up to you," he said.

"If it can preserve my mental state and satisfy my need for freedom…"

title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘The cardiac Knicks find a way’
author: Antonio Losada
text:
The same we thought we’d never see GTA VI hit the proverbial shelves…

Here’s a bunch of quotes and comments coming off another Knicks dub in Toronto.

On Darko Rajaković’s coaching and the Raptors’ defensive intensity:

“Darko does a heckuva job… those guys play hard, really good defensively, give us fits.”

On Jalen Brunson’s late four-point play creating the separation needed to beat Toronto:

“That created the separation that we needed to be able to put them away. So just a big shot. It was one of those things where the play broke down, and we kept looking for an opportunity while spacing the floor. And Jalen found one and let it fly.”

On the Knicks’ late-game execution and contributions from Towns, Anunoby, Bridges and Shamet:

“I thought our execution, especially down the stretch, the last few minutes of the game, was at a pretty high level, on both ends of the floor, but particularly offensively. Our pacing, our spacing, our screening — we took care of the basketball down the stretch.

“We got a lot of different guys that produced in a lot of different ways tonight. Obviously, KAT continues to be a double-double machine. OG [Anunoby] was our defensive player of the game. … Mikal was good for us, especially down the stretch. And Landry Shamet was huge.”

On his improved relationship with Karl-Anthony Towns and the importance of adapting his coaching philosophy:

“It’s just part of being around each other. You hope your relationship with everybody grows. That’s not gonna always happen but you hope it does. KAT’s got a really good feel of how to play the game. Obviously he’s a perennial All-Star. So those things you’ve always got to take into account when it comes to trying to listen or try to adapt more to what their style of play is.

“As a head coach — come in, it’s your first year, and you have an idea what you want to do. Sometimes it doesn’t fit. Offensively, or defensively. And that’s when you’ve got to pivot. And so we kept pivoting and pivoting and building until we found a nice little groove. We feel pretty good about each other right now.”

On recovering from the ankle injury scare after his four-point play:

“Adrenaline was pumping, and went back out there.”

On Josh Hart and Mikal Bridges regaining confidence and contributing to the Knicks’ success:

“This is a huge night for them, the way they played. They’re gaining confidence every single night. They’re going to continue to do great things for us and they’re only going to get better.”

On the Knicks rediscovering their ability to win close games:

“A lot of times when we get in games like that, especially last year, the cardiac Knicks find a way.”

On gaining Mike Brown’s trust and having more input in the team’s strategy:

“It’s more familiarity with the system and building that trust with Mike where he can trust me with things I see and say, which started in the playoffs. So building off that this year. Having more input and him hearing me out.”

On acting as a second coach and collaborating with Brown during games:

“Him trusting me like a second coach. Me and him are always coaching with each other in the game, looking at game plans and plays and maybe ideologies and things I see that can help our team win, especially in close games. Working with him and coaching on the floor. It’s been great. It’s been fun.”

On how his relationship with Brown has improved since the championship run:

“We just grew. We’ve grown with each other. And obviously there’s trust that has to be established and both of us trust each other a lot. And the last playoff run showed it. So just building off that trust and the relationship that was built in the playoffs and having it make our team better this year.”

On Jose Alvarado’s professionalism and importance to the Knicks’ locker room:

“Jose is a consummate professional. He’s probably one of the best locker room guys we have, and one of the best people we have on the bench. His energy, just his presence, with a jersey on or a warmup on, it means more for this team than what the stats show.”

On his recent mental struggles:

“Has been kicking my ass for a couple weeks.”

On stepping up his game on Tuesday after struggling through a few games:

“I think it was a step in the right direction. I think I’m obviously getting into the flow, into the rhythm of things, but today was a step in the right direction. Still a lot to improve on, but you got to start stacking days at some point.”

On how his contract situation can amplify the pressure of poor performances:

“That’s a low-hanging fruit. Sometimes some of those things amplify because you’re in a contract year, essentially. It’s human nature.

“It’s in the back of your mind, and when you start focusing on those things, negative outcomes happen.”

On trying to overcome his struggles and improve his mindset:

“When you’re in the middle of it, there’s not much that can really help. At the end of the day, you just have to go out there. And I think today I had a little bit of a better spirit.”

On the negative thought patterns that have affected his performances:

“I’m struggling to shoot the ball, but it’s one of those things where you start looking at the negatives and that’s all you see. You don’t see some of the positives. Then it’s a snowball effect. One thing happens and you’re trying to get yourself out of a hole that you’re not giving yourself the ability to get out of. It’s about playing with that joyful spirit, looking at things half full instead of half empty.”

On dealing with physical and mental challenges simultaneously:

“For me, this (rough patch) is a little harder because I’m trying to get the mental aspect right and the physical aspect right. It can be easier when you’re just dealing with one of those things. … I’m battling both of those things. I’m trying to give myself a little bit of grace with that.”

On maintaining a positive attitude despite losing his place in the Knicks’ rotation:

“I think it’s more how I was raised [by] my parents. Treat people how you want to be treated. Sometimes the situation isn’t going to be what you want. You can’t control certain things and control what you can and that’s your attitude, your energy every day. So I try to do that.

“I’m human, I have days where it’s not going to be all lovey-dovey. But I always tell myself, ‘Whether I’m not playing or not, I got the best seats in the house.’ And I get to support my teammates. So I try to go with that mindset as best I can and my teammates allow me to be myself.”

On the viral clip showing him comforting Mikal Bridges on the bench:

“[Mikal] is fine. We are all human. The camera caught us that time, but I probably do stuff like that 100 times during a game.”

On staying prepared for opportunities after falling out of the rotation:

“The season is long. I’ve been on the other side. When I first got in the league [in 2021], I wasn’t even touching the court. Then eventually I got to touch the court and get some reps in and played a huge role in the rotation.

“Sometimes you get out of it. The only way to get back is stay ready because an opportunity is going to come, you just don’t know when. So that’s the hardest thing is the guessing game of when that will happen. But you work, work and work and trust that it will come in the end of the day.”

On how close the Raptors came to beating the Knicks in their previous meeting:

“After rewatching and rewatching and rewatching film, we played against the NBA champions and, in my three-and-a-half years here as coach, that’s when we came the closest to beating them. We’re getting better. Just one free throw and the game is completely different.”

title: Football Daily | From Cincinnati to Manchester: Pochettino in a hurry to paint town red
author: Barry Glendenning
text:
With his team mired in the relegation zone and a massive match at Liverpool this weekend, Mauricio Pochettino has been understandably busy since being appointed head coach of Manchester United. Unfortunately for Old Trafford regulars, the small print of his contract meant the Argentinian was tied up masterminding victory for USA USA USA in the second leg of their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final against Haiti when he ought to have been in Carrington moving red magnets around a tactics board in front of Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo and Harry Maguire.

The match in Cincinnati was ostensibly a dead rubber, given the hosts kicked off with a 6-0 lead. However, the conditions of Pochettino’s release clause dictated he had to remain in charge until finishing his post-match media duties at the TQL Stadium. Like an errant spouse having one last dinner with their put-upon partner while their lover waits outside the restaurant with the engine running, Pochettino was unable to make his excuses and leave until the bill was settled. It was no surprise that his new role came up during his exit interview. In a playful exchange with DaMarcus Beasley, who spent a season on loan at Manchester City during the (Ben) Thatcher era, something of a gauntlet was thrown down to the departing boss. “Manchester is blue, it will always be blue,” honked the former international, who may be unaware of his former club’s disgrace and potentially imminent relegation to the North West Counties League.

“No way, you will see,” chuckled Pochettino by way of response. “Give me time. Give me time and that is going to change, for sure.” While the future colour scheme of football in Manchester almost certainly lies more in the hands of the three-person independent panel who will decide City’s fate after finding them guilty of industrial scale financial shenanigans, Pochettino assured fans he and his staff will do their bit to ensure the city will be painted red. “We are excited because the new challenge is a big challenge,” he whooped. “But at the same time, it’s the adrenaline that you want to feel. We are going to have a different job, but we have the experience to deal with that. We know that it is not a situation that deserves to be at a club like Manchester United and for the fanbase. The fanbase is amazing.”

Considering they’ve been flirting with Pochettino for nine years, most United fans will be unconcerned by his eventual arrival being delayed by an extra couple of days but, with that game against Liverpool to prepare for, the 54-year-old wasted little time in hightailing it to the airport and boarding a private jet for his new home. Upon arrival, he is expected to oversee his first training session, an event Sky Sports News has melodramatically anticipated using a serene, high-budget cinematic aesthetic that captures our Argentinian hero gazing longingly into a Manchester sunset. It’s a majestic, blockbuster shot that has rightfully become the subject of no end of online mockery. Football Daily wonders if we’ll see a contrasting shot on Sunday, when the Sky cameras cut to Pochettino staring in wide-eyed horror as Liverpool spank yet another goal past his side’s hapless defence.

Seixas, Pidcock, Kuss: Who Stays and Who Goes in 2027?
author: ahood
text:
Seixas will be the center of transfer intrigue in 2027. (Photo: Anne-Christine POUJOULAT / AFP)

Everyone wants Paul Seixas . In 2027, they might get their chance.

Seixas’ contract expires after next season, and the mad scramble for his contract is already starting to rumble.

He’s not alone. Tom Pidcock , Sepp Kuss , and Lenny Martinez are the other marquee names off-contract in 2027 who will be headlining next year’s high-stakes transfer market.

A few riders are still looking for spots in 2027 after their deals ran out this year, including Primož Roglič and Max Schachmann, among a dozen others.

For everyone else, attention is already shifting to the 2027-28 transfer season, which could rival last year’s upheaval , when Remco Evenepoel, Juan Ayuso and Oscar Onley all ripped up existing deals and swapped jerseys.

Tadej Pogačar and Jonas Vingegaard are both under contract and secure at the top of the hierarchy. For anyone else hoping to catch up, a few big names could make the difference.

For this year, it’s going to be all about the Seixas Sweepstakes. And what he does will shape the entire market .

The gossip will start at the team camps next month in Spain and be hyped by leaks, exclusives, and conjecture all the way to the Tour de France.

Here are the big transfer names to watch in 2027:

There won’t be a bigger transfer saga in 2027 than Paul Seixas. And there might not be a bigger price tag, either, if this year’s $13 million rumored offer comes true.

The 20-year-old French phenom more than proved his quality in a rock-solid WorldTour campaign, becoming the youngest-ever winner of Il Lombardia and nearly hitting the podium in his Tour de France debut with fourth overall.

He’s the top name off-contract in 2027, and nearly every team has reached out . Visma-Lease a Bike and Pinarello Q36.5 are already circling, with Q36.5 reportedly putting a massive €13 million per year on the table for 2028.

There’s talk Seixas could target victory at the Giro d’Italia in May rather than return to a less favorable Tour route and another July trying to hold Pogačar’s wheel.

The bigger question is whether Decathlon can convince him to stay beyond 2027.

The team is certainly trying. It has recruited more stage racing support, notably Pavel Sivakov, to give its franchise rider more company when the road kicks up.

Seixas seems happy at Decathlon and has chosen to honor his final year of his current deal . That buys the team another few months to prove he can chase cycling’s biggest prizes without changing jerseys.

With suitors lining up, the ball is in his court. Seixas could name his price and take his pick, but salary might not settle this one.

Can Decathlon give him everything he needs in coaching, training, nutrition, equipment, and aerodynamics to match the super teams?

Keeping Seixas will take more than paying him like a Tour winner. The deciding factor will be if Decathlon can convince him he can become one there.

Visma will have nearly half its roster out of contract at the end of 2027, so the team will be busy locking down its leaders and shopping for fresh legs.

One rider it probably won’t have to worry about losing is Sepp Kuss. It’s hard to imagine the “Eagle of Durango” in any other jersey.

Kuss is a team anchor, a huge fan favorite, and the last American to win a grand tour with his 2023 Vuelta a España victory.

Fans might still want more “GC Kuss,” and Visma knows how valuable he is.

Kuss is essential to the Killer Bees ethos. Across the team’s latest run of grand tour success, he has been part of every winning lineup except Simon Yates’ 2025 Giro d’Italia squad.

And he’s still putting numbers on the board, including a Giro stage win to complete the “grand tour” sweep of stages, and finishing fifth at the Vuelta.

Kuss admits he doesn’t like the pressure of leadership, so he probably won’t be chasing a big-money contract to be a GC leader on another team.

The bigger question might be how much longer Kuss wants to keep doing it.

A recent at-home video offered a glimpse of a happy life in Andorra with his wife and child. So far, there’s no hint he’s ready to trade mountain passes for more afternoons at home. His favored program of racing all three grand tours also fits his work-life balance.

If both sides want it, a “forever” contract like those signed by Wout van Aert and Marianne Vos would seem a fitting way to keep him in yellow and black.

It’s equally hard to imagine Pidcock going anywhere else.

His blockbuster move to Pinarello Q36.5 was one of the top transfers two years ago.

Since then, Pidcock’s more than earned his spot as the team’s franchise rider. Perhaps 2026 was missing one big win, but taking Pogačar to the line at Milan-San Remo, another mountain bike world title, and a top 10 in the Tour de France confirmed his chops.

Pinarello Q36.5 remains one of the most aggressive teams on the rider market , picking up 10 new riders coming into 2027.

Doug Ryder, with the backing of team owners, is pushing the pedal for WorldTour classification by the next round at the end of 2028.

For Pidcock, his spot is secure, so it will be a question of hammering out the details on how many zeroes are attached to his next deal.

The team gives him the schedule he likes, plus carves out time for his MTB side quest. With the LA Olympic Games coming up, Pidcock won’t be wanting to swap teams.

Unless someone can convince him otherwise.

If it weren’t for Seixas, Lenny Martinez would have finished the 2026 Tour de France as the top French rider, in fifth.

That will give him some bargaining power coming into 2027.

At 23, his stock is still rising, even if Seixas has grabbed the spotlight as France’s next great Tour hope.

The son of Olympic mountain bike champion Miguel Martinez and grandson of Tour king of the mountains winner Mariano Martinez has the family pedigree. The consistency is still lacking, but the first half of 2026 confirmed his potential.…

title: The factors behind the abortive 2030 F1 rules announcement
Israel delays building contracts for West Bank settlement after UK sanctions
author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
text:
Attorney general says E1 settlement decision should not be taken by caretaker government led by Netanyahu

Israel has postponed issuing contracts for the construction of a large settlement on the West Bank seen as likely to render a two-state solution unviable, days after the UK imposed sanctions against building firms operating in the area.

Israeli diplomats insisted the move was not in response to the measures from Downing Street . Gali Baharav-Miara, the attorney general, said any decision on settlement expansion should not be taken by the caretaker government led by Benjamin Netanyahu but by whatever new administration was formed.

She ordered the Israel land authority and ministry of housing not to open the tender process. Israeli diplomats suggested the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband , had acted prematurely on Monday in sanctioning the eight construction firms. But UK diplomats believe the growing political pressure on Israel over settlements, including from US Democrats, is having an impact.

The deferral puts the E1 settlement expansion in the mix for any coalition negotiations. The leader of the Change bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, seen as Israel’s most likely next prime minister, has been clear in opposing violent settler activity, as has the newly elected Knesset speaker, Matan Kahana, an ally of Eisenkot.

Eisenkot has also opposed the E1 settlement expansion, describing it as a mistake likely to alienate international opinion. He said of the plan: “I recall that Netanyahu himself opposed this for a long time, and due to coalition pressure, he gave in and approved it.”

The EI settlement expansion, due to have been announced on Thursday, has long been seen as qualitatively different since the land – between Jerusalem and Ma’aleh Adumim, a West Bank settlement city of nearly 40,000 residents – bisects the West Bank and cuts it off from East Jerusalem.

Miliband has said it would mark the death knell of a future Palestinian state. The UK, along with a group of European countries, has recently recognised Palestine , and the preservation of a two-state solution has been described as the north star of Labour policy towards the region.

The construction tender was published for more than 3,401 housing units in the area. At the beginning of November, the Israel Defense Forces began demolishing homes in a Bedouin community within the E1 area.

Israel has already enforced the downgrading of the UK consulate in East Jerusalem as a reprisal for Miliband’s decision in September to try to end trade links with the illegal settlements.

Bennett said: “The British Labour government’s hostility, bias and one-sided approach are particularly glaring given its failure to take any action against the Palestinian Authority, which continues to encourage terrorism through financial payments, promote incitement in its education system and engage in illegal construction in violation of signed agreements.”

Although the Israeli election was largely fought on domestic security-related issues, Eisenkot seems to be more sensitive to the implications of Israel’s crumbling global reputation, and the need to make efforts to be seen to be listening to the criticism.

If he becomes prime minister, Eisenkot will, indirectly at least, also have to take account of the views of the Arab parties even if these parties are not going to become members of the government.

The group Peace Now welcomed the attorney general’s decision: “A government that lost the elections is not permitted to exploit its final days in power to advance destructive moves that will endanger Israel’s future and its international standing.

Construction in E1 is liable to eliminate the possibility of a two-state solution and drag Israel into a severe diplomatic crisis and international sanctions. The AG’s decision is an important step, but the struggle is not over yet.”

title: 'I'd say it’s costing people’s lives' – Safer technology is here, so why hasn’t the cycling industry implemented tougher helmet testing yet?
author: Emma Cole
text:
Helmet safety awareness and the danger of head injuries from cycling crashes is growing, so why haven't helmet standards changed for years, and what is being done to improve the technology that protects our brains as cyclists?

A test for how helmets deal with rotational head impacts was created and published in 2024, but two years on, the committee tasked with setting a pass mark is yet to agree whether, or how, to require it, and so many helmets are missing a key standard of safety and protection.

Mips (multi-directional impact protection system) technology has long been the market leader in rotational impact technology, and you'll see its yellow sticker and protective system on many helmets. Mips technology is fitted between the inner padding and outer shell of the helmet, and allows for slippage and movement that helps reduce the rotational impact transferred to the wearer's head.

Whilst popular, Mips is not the be-all and end-all of helmet safety technology, and new externally-fitted solutions like RLS have come into play in recent years, but the helmet industry – and riders – are still waiting on a universal standard.

We spoke to leading figures from helmet technology manufacturers, helmet brands and independent testing bodies to find out what is standing between the industry and a better safety standard, and what the future of helmet safety might look like.

Why rotational impact testing matters

Cycling helmets sold in Europe are certified to European Standard EN 1078, which was last updated in 2012, nearly a decade and a half ago. It tests only linear, straight-on impacts.

This is noteworthy because when the head hits the ground at an angle, it twists, and the brain is stretched and sheared because of this rotation. This can damage the nerve fibres that carry signals around the brain, as well as blood vessels, resulting in concussion or more severe damage such as a TBI.

This is why many believe in the importance of testing cycling helmets at angled or oblique impacts, as this is more representative of real-world bike collisions – and indeed rotational impact is often more dangerous and more severe than a straight-on knock.

Innovating external solutions

Despite the lack of a European Standard or wider requirements for helmets to also protect against rotational impacts, plenty of manufacturers, scientists, and innovators are working to create systems that better protect riders and get this technology into more helmets.

The Release Layer System (RLS) is a newer rotational impact technology which works by having panels bonded to the outside layer of the helmet which move on polycarbonate bearings. Upon impact, these panels absorb energy and release from the helmet, reducing the amount of rotational energy transferred to the rider’s head.

I was invited to see this technology firsthand at the RLS facility in London, complete with a testing drop tower they use to assess the impact helmets absorb.

RLS says its technology lowers the risk of a brain injury like concussion from 64% to 9% when compared to a standard road helmet.

"Because the technology is on the outside, the moment you make an impact, the technology is able to instantaneously work rather than being in those microseconds absorbed and then having to do the work on the inside," explains James Cook, CEO of RLS.

"When you increase the energy, a lot of solutions don’t work very well because there's too much pressure. That's where actually a bearing solution is really good because bearings have been used for high pressure."

Cook adds that the panels are designed to survive everyday knocks and will only come apart under a significant impact.

RLS grew out of HEXR , a helmet brand Cook co-founded, which it now uses to test the technology.

While Mips has long dominated the market with its internal slip layer system, there is a consensus that external solutions like RLS could also work well, or even better.

"Reducing friction on the outside is a better idea than reducing it on the inside," says Alessandro Cernicchi, R&D director at helmet manufacturer Kask.

"If you want to redirect energy, a good way to do that is on the outside of the helmet because you have quite a big surface there and you can create a big movement and so on," says Max Strandwitz, CEO of Mips.

Mips developed its own external concept in 2017 called Impact Shield. However, Strandwitz believes that external solutions can be too sensitive.

"We were a little bit reluctant to release the Impact Shield because as soon as you have solutions on the outside of the helmet, they become very sensitive. If you drop it or if you bump into something, all of a sudden, the technology is out."

Despite his hesitations, Strandwitz says Mips might reconsider an external solution.

For now, Mips’ market position remains formidable. He says Mips is adding its technology to almost one new helmet every working day across all categories, including snow, motorcycle and industrial helmets, with cycling making up roughly two-thirds of its business.

The power of the yellow dot sticker is reflected in Fizik’s decision to enter the helmet market with Mips.

"Being new into a category, we haven't got years of people telling good stories about our helmets, and we knew what a well-respected brand name could do in terms of entering a new market," says George Huxford, senior marketing manager at Fizik.

The elusive mandatory test

There are two main European Committee for Standardisation (CEN) working groups related to implementing a rotational impact standard for helmets.

Working Group 11 (WG11) set a rotational test method called EN 17950, with a new headform – the dummy used for testing – which was published in 2024. This headform is regarded as more representative of a human head. It took over 10 years for the group to agree on this, and even now there are some disagreements.

Working Group 4 is revising EN 1078, the standard to which every cycling helmet sold in Europe is certified and may establish a pass/fail mark for helmets with regard to rotational impact. It is this revision which would mandate that all helmets be rotationally tested as per EN 17950 and the headform which should be used in testing.

The working groups are made up of manufacturers, brands, ingredient technology companies, universities, test labs, governments and consumer groups, all of whom will be impacted by what is agreed, which may be having a disproportionate effect on the decisions these groups are or aren't taking.

"It’s really a shame that standards have not yet adopted rotation, and I think it is the elephant in the room," says Professor Mazdak Ghajari of Imperial College London, who co-authored WG11's research on the new headform.

"Well, I may upset some of my colleagues on the working groups, but the truth is that over 80% [of parties sitting on the committees] are manufacturers," he adds. "They are members of the committee for good reasons; we cannot set a standard that they cannot meet or which costs them a massive amount of money.

"But at the same time, they told me that they spent 80% of their budget and R&D on optimising products for the current standard. Now imagine if there is something new, then they have to inject new money into understanding how their product would perform so obviously there is a lot of inertia."

"There is a lot of politics which I think doesn't belong in the regulatory body for safety standards," adds Strandwitz, also noting the difference between the US and European approaches.

"In [the] US, it's a much hotter potato, and they are moving and will probably move a lot quicker," he says. "In Europe, you are still having some that are a bit conservative, and that think rotation is not a big problem.

"My experience is that it's seriously conflicted," echoes Cook, who sat on WG11. "People are not just thinking about how they protect people; they’re also thinking about how they protect the business.

"There's a deadline that the European Commission sets, but then there are ways in which the working groups can collectively not align to either extend the timeline or push things back, and that's effectively what's going on. It’s just the can is being kicked down the road again, and again, and again, and I’d say it’s costing people’s lives.

"We're seriously keen to try and push to have at least a standard that recognises rotation, but then also push to have a pass/fail criteria that means that more helmets are going to be safer on the road."

However, Cernicchi at Kask views conflict within the group as expected and healthy, since all stakeholders are represented.

Cernicchi believes a cautious approach is best.

"It's kind of a revolution in the way we are testing helmets; we've been testing helmets for years with linear impact, and now we are proposing to introduce rotation. You want to do it very, very carefully."

The headform, the dummy used in testing, is meant to reflect a human head and was a major sticking point for WG11 members to agree on. Headforms have different coefficients of friction from one another and thus produce different results.

Kask still uses the EN 960 headform in its testing but says it plans to transition to EN 17950 headforms from 2027.

"The EN 17950 standard is still not perfect, so we still have to work on it to make it perfect, and then we can start adopting rotational methods for certifying helmets according to the product standards," says Cernicchi.

He says EN 17950 headforms made by different manufacturers produced results up to about 10% different, and experts want that narrowed before rotation can go into EN 1078.

"We have to rewrite it to have narrower tolerances before we can introduce [the] rotational method in the 1078 and all the other product standards."

Any new headform also comes at a cost to manufacturers, which could also be a factor behind the slow implementation of more accurate headforms.

"If Europe agrees to approve a new headform, it will mean an investment of somewhere around €20,000 to €25,000 for a lot of companies because you need to invest in a new headform," says Strandwitz.

"This should have been done already a long time ago. If you look at the EN 960 headform, it's 30 years old, and it's not biofidelic. It's a magnesium headform without the nose, and it looks extremely flat."

Independent ratings and testing

There’s another layer of complexity around helmet testing and standards, and that's who pays for the testing and research.

Brands often test their own technology in-house. Kask, for example, has its own testing protocol, WG11, and now has its own in-house testing laboratory. RLS has its own drop tower and publishes side-by-side test videos, while Strandwitz says Mips runs 15,000 to 18,000 tests a year but doesn’t publish them publicly.

Strandwitz doesn’t think that brands publishing their own test results is enough, and retains some scepticism about the results we do see.

"For me, it will be strange if you, as the market leader, say: 'Look what we have done at home!' Who would publish a test that doesn’t come out well?" he says. "If you have a technology that is good enough, you can rely on third-party testing, and that’s what we do."

Professor Ghajari launched Hiper two years ago as an independent safety rating system, developed by researchers at Imperial College London and funded by The Road Safety Trust.

Hiper buys each one of the helmets it tests and does not accept money from brands, which Ghajari says helps maintain independence.

"It's very important because even manufacturers tell me that they can send a helmet to rating that is different to the helmet they send to the market," he says. "It is a known fact and another elephant in the room."

Ghajari adds that Hiper’s ratings are meant to sit alongside the standard as they provide consumers with safety information beyond the minimum, which is important as a high price point does not equate to a safer helmet.…

title: Typical energy bill forecast to go up by £443 a year from January as inflation rate rises again
text:
Gas and electricity bills are forecast to jump by £443 a year from January as energy costs continue to push up the UK's inflation rate.

The annual price cap on gas and elecrtricity is predicted to rise by 26% in the new year, according to researchers at consultancy Cornwall Insight. Energy regulator Ofgem will announce the new cap next Wednesday, 25 November.

A sharp jump means inflation is at risk of continuing to rise - official data revealed prices rose 3.6% in the year to October, up from 3.5% in September mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices.

Inflation is at its highest rate in a year as energy prices have accelerated largely due to the US-Israel war with Iran.

In response to prices surging, the Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in three years earlier this month, in a bid to slow inflation to its target of 2%.

Interest rates increased from 3.75% to 4%, and the Bank signalled a further rise could be likely unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved.

Higher interest rates lift the cost of borrowing for some mortgages, loans and credit cards, but can also lead to a better return on savings.

Emma Reynolds, chief secretary to the Treasury, said the government was providing help for households with energy costs.

VAT has been cut on electricity bills to zero until next July and the government will also hand £100 to 20 million homes in January.

But with annual household energy bills forecast to reach £2,166, Cornwall Insight's retail markets principal, Craig Lowrey, said that "ultimately this support can only chip away at the edges of a bill that continues to be pushed up by events in the Middle East".

Sophie, who manages a cafe at the Old Boat Corner community centre in Brighton, told the BBC she watches her smart meter at home "like a hawk".

"I'm very conscious of the cost of energy, and it is having an impact on how we function in the home as a family," she said.

"I try to cook using the oven a lot less than I used to. We haven't got the heating on yet in our household. We're just like 'wear more layers'. We've got electric blankets on the sofa."

Shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, said four successive rises in the inflation rate was down to the UK's "soaring energy costs" and Labour's decision to "hike taxes and employment costs".

Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the ONS, said fuel prices were "once again a major contributor" to the increase in the inflation rate in October.

Rising energy prices can lead to more expensive food and staples for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs.

Earlier this month, the Bank of England said there had been "limited evidence" of this, with some firms absorbing cost increases and accepting lower profit margins.

But Fitzner said on Wednesday: "Annual costs of both raw materials and goods leaving factories continue to climb, driven by higher crude oil and petrol prices, respectively."

Petrol prices rose by 5.2p per litre between September and October, the ONS said, with the average price last month hitting 174.7p per litre - the highest since August 2022.

Diesel prices, meanwhile, reached the highest price since records began 30 years ago, averaging 199.5p per litre in October.

But the ONS said price inflation in restaurants and cafes had slowed last month, and that prices had fallen on average for hotels.

And food price inflation rose by 0.9%, the slowest pace in five years.

Core inflation, which strips out energy and food costs, and services inflation were little changed on last month. The figure is closely watched by the Bank of England when setting interest rates.

It could mean the Bank opts to hold off on a further rate rise in December, though policymakers believe inflation could peak at 4.9% in the middle of next year and not return to 2% until 2028.

In an "adverse scenario", where the US-Iran war could escalate further and send oil prices higher, inflation could reach 6.2% in 2027, it has suggested.

A spokesperson for the Bank said it decided to raise rates two weeks ago to "limit how much higher energy costs affect other prices, and will continue to set interest rates to make sure inflation returns to the 2% target and stays there".

title: Heating bills, chocolate and cat food: What the inflation figures mean for you
text:
Nobody will be celebrating the fact that prices in the UK are rising at the fastest pace for a year.

Add to that an expectation of higher household energy bills and sharpening price increases and things look grim for everyone.

But there are some signs of hope that may take the edge off the rising cost of living. Here's how.

That headline is not missing a decimal point. The latest prediction for the increase in domestic energy prices in the new year is, indeed, 26%.

Millions of homes in England, Scotland and Wales are on tariffs affected by regulator Ofgem's price cap, which is set every three months. The next change for January will be officially announced next Wednesday, 25 November.

Energy consultancy Cornwall Insight, which has a good track record with its predictions, suggests that a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity will pay £2,166 a year - that's an increase of £443 from current levels.

Not all energy use for the year is between January and March, but a big chunk is owing to the cold, dark days and nights.

How much you pay depends on your use, with heavy users of gas likely to be the hardest hit.

The government has promised a £100 payment for people living in homes in council tax bands A to D in England to help cover winter energy costs. Other nations are planning similar support.

The latest inflation data shows that government assistance can have an impact on the general rate of inflation , external , as recorded by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

Domestic energy prices rose by nearly 4% in October, but this was offset in inflationary terms by a cut in VAT on electricity bills.

While the rate of inflation in general was 3.6% in the year to October, food prices only went up by 0.9%.

It is partly the result of intense competition between the supermarkets. Like many retailers, they are facing higher costs but are not passing that onto their customers in full.

There may be some scars from the recent cost-of-living spike here. Shoppers suffered a period during the big rise in inflation in 2022-23 when food prices rocketed.

Those higher prices are embedded. While food prices overall aren't coming down now, they aren't rising anywhere near as fast as back then.

The detail here is very interesting. Take chocolate: world cocoa prices are down since 2024, and now chocolate prices are falling - down 2.9%, according to the latest data.

But the ONS has also pointed to cat food as one, albeit small, driver of the faster rate of rising prices.

Should high energy and fuel costs - which are driving the rising rate of inflation - persist, there are questions over whether the cost of producing and transporting food also goes up, and the chances of that higher cost being passed on to consumers are greater.

Economists have been closely studying whether there are any signs of those so-called second-round effects - where an initial price shock spreads to wages, services and broader consumer prices. So far, there are relatively few.

If prices rise then it takes a bigger chunk of people's income and so has a deeper impact on those whose finances are already stretched, so the latest data on food prices is good news for many people.

Typical energy bill forecast to go up by £443 a year from January as inflation rate rises again

One set of economists who will consider whether there is evidence of second-round effects are the nine people who set interest rates, which heavily influences the cost of borrowing money - such as mortgages - as well as the returns people get on savings.

The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee meets again in December and, after that, in February.

Having just raised interest rates - for the first time in more than three years - to 4%, there's a widespread expectation among analysts that another hike is to come.

To be clear, we don't know if and when that will happen for sure.

The case for an increase would be if prices continue to accelerate. The Bank will want to slow that down.

The case against would be price rises remaining relatively confined to energy-related costs. Any easing of Middle East tensions could limit price rises without Bank of England intervention.

As far as wages are concerned, the latest official data suggests that rising prices are largely covered by rising pay.

That is an average - so is not true for everyone - but how long it remains the case may be key to how deep upcoming price rises cut into our personal finances.

title: Energy price cap rise: how to switch providers
author: Hilary Osborne Consumer and money editor
text:
It is possible to switch to a better tariff and save money despite the forecast rise next year

Average energy bill in Great Britain predicted to rise to £2,166

The energy price cap in Great Britain looks likely to go up by 26% in January . But your bills might not have to rise by the same amount. If you are paying a tariff that matches the price cap you could save by switching to something lower. And if you do it now, you could make a substantial saving.

Providers are offering fixed tariffs that work out up to £407 below the estimated price cap, according to price comparison website uSwitch. It’s worth noting that it’s the price of the energy you use that is fixed, not your bill – so you will still be charged according to what you use.

title: Castelli Alpha 150 jacket review: Warm and comfortable, but not right for the deep freeze
author: william.jones@futurenet.com (Will Jones)
text:
Castelli’s jacket range has gone on a fair old journey in recent years. The Gabba and Perfetto have been overhauled, and everything is now PFAS-free.

The Alpha 150 is the Italian brand’s most wintery and most expensive outer layer, featuring an inbuilt fluffy body warmer to really seal you in and, I presume, seal a top spot in my guide to the best winter cycling jackets .

I’ve been testing it out throughout last winter, and through a fortuitously timed cold snap in recent weeks that has left the air thick with freezing mists and rich fog. I do like it as a jacket, but like many recent Castelli options I’ve been testing out, the suggested temperature range is perhaps a little too cold for reality. The flip side is that the breathability is excellent, so as long as you don’t stop, it’s less of an issue.

Eight colours for such an expensive jacket does feel like a recipe for the unpopular ones to go on sale eventually, but they are all at least part of a pleasing spectrum.

For my part, I tested out the ‘mango mojito’ colour, which is a posh way of saying ‘yellow’. It’s the platonic ideal of yellow; primary, bright, unfussy, and I was glad of it in the gloom versus the more subdued Assos jackets I’ve also been testing alongside it.

The form is tailored but not skin-tight, with enough room to layer up a little bit underneath, at least with a thicker long-sleeve jersey and a winter base layer . You get a high, fleece-lined collar and very neat cuffs that feature a tight, stretchy synthetic cuff that surrounds the wrist, and a looser yellow main fabric over the top that I’m sure does little practically but certainly improves the aesthetics.

Open up the main double zip, either through the big, easy-to-pull-with-gloves-on toggle at the top or the normal zip tab at the bottom, and you’ll reveal a Polartec Alpha inbuilt gilet. The rear panel is free-floating, attached only at the sides and top so it articulates more easily and I assume compresses less.

The front is two simple panels with a low-cut neckline, so that you can use the main zip to cool the neck or accommodate a neck warmer, and secured by a smaller one-way zip. I could do with this also being 2-way, for reasons of pocket access, but I imagine Castelli envisioned it being used perhaps with just a deep winter base layer underneath.

The main fabric is Castelli’s exclusive ‘150g Polartec® AirCore™ electrospun air-permeable membrane’, which is alleged to be windproof while also remaining highly breathable. To this end, it is. Castelli also claims it can ‘stand up to everything except all-day driving rain’. It can’t. If it’s going to rain, wear something else; a waterproof jacket, perhaps.

It is relatively lightweight in feel. My size medium tips the scales at 324g, 70g less than an equivalent Assos jacket that I’ve been testing, but spread over your whole torso you’re not really going to notice that difference. The relative softness and flexibility of that Aircore outer fabric does make it lighter compared to stiffer, hardier options.

At the back, you get a reflective piping sewn under the standard three rear pockets and above a stretchy, neoprene-like waistband that is dropped far enough to cover even non-modern jerseys, though again, I suspect this is meant to just go over a base layer.

This is a good jacket; I do want to get that on record first. I do think the suggested temperature range is a little ambitious, however, and I don’t think you can realistically use this comfortably in anything below about 5ºC if you plan on stopping for any time at all.

The issue comes not from the added cosy insulation, but from that AirCore fabric. I had the same issues with the DoDiCi jacket, and my colleague Josh had with the previous Perfetto RoS 3 ; it’s just a little breathable, so you don’t keep as much heat in as you think you will and you get a little colder than you’d like.

A few commutes around 6º, with a merino base layer and a merino long-sleeve jersey underneath, it started to feel a little on the cool side, and when things hovered around zero, I often found myself reaching for my Albion Ultralight Insulated Jacket to slip over the top as a breathability modifier.

The wind resistance was perfectly good; I never felt like the breeze was scything through the fabric even on fast descents, so I do think it’s just a function of just how breathable the outer is. If you’re doing higher-output riding in the winter, then it does make more sense, but for those longer, steadier winter miles it’s just not quite right.

That aside, when I did get the temperature right, I found it was really excellent. When you use it when it’s a little warmer - somewhere between about 7 and 12 degrees (44-54 degrees F) - on less intense rides, it keeps you just the right temperature, and the added breathability means when you get hot on climbs you don’t immediately get drenched and then freeze.

If you do get a little toasty, it’s very easy to ventilate yourself back into a comfortable range. The interior Polartec Alpha gilet thing is so breathable at the front that when you unzip the main outer zip you can feel the wind cooling you immediately.

I found a few centimetres at the top and bottom of the zip undone was often sufficient to keep me where I wanted if I was cooking a little, but on the whole this was never a jacket I ever overheated in, and I feel like I’d have to try really hard and layer very badly to get it wrong to the point where I’d become a sweaty mess at the side of the road. The most I ever really had to do was take a neck warmer off.

The cut is also excellent. The sleeves are long enough to not expose my wrists, even as a very gangly chap, and there’s enough room that I never felt constricted even with an additional jersey between my jacket and my base layer. I don’t think you’ll have a great time if you try and wear a thicker mid layer, as you can do with some of the Assos deep winter layers I’ve tested, but a thick winter jersey is totally doable.

This brings me to the pockets; the three on the actual jacket itself are great, easy to access and roomy enough to house things like a light waterproof shell or a pair of gloves with ease alongside the usual suspects.

My main annoyance comes with the fact that the internal fluffy gilet zip isn’t 2-way. I almost always wear a jersey under my winter jackets, even if it’s just a thin one. It gives me three extra pockets, as much as anything else, but with this zip arrangement, you just can’t get in easily. It’s a minor gripe, but a gripe nonetheless.

At $645 or £360 it’s a very expensive jacket, significantly more than the likes of the exceptional Assos Equipe R Winter Jacket , one I would argue is superior in performance across a wider range of temperatures.

While I did (and still do) very much enjoy using it, given I found it better suited to longer, lower-intensity riding in warmer conditions than advertised, for many of you I suspect you can get the same level of insulation for a lot less outlay, and while you won’t have the same breathability, this won’t necessarily be such a problem for slower cold-weather riding unless you run very hot indeed.

Castelli’s Alpha 150 jacket may be the warmest the brand makes, but if you’re going anywhere near actual freezing conditions, then I suggest this isn’t the jacket to reach for, as it’s just too breathable to keep you at a comfortable temperature.

For longer, lower-intensity riding at high single figures, it’s dreamy, comfortable, good-looking, and well finished, but it’s a lot of money to drop on a jacket like this when cheaper options will do the same thing in many cases.

Exactly what I'd want in a winter jacket. Close but with enough room for a choice few key layers.

It's simply not as warm as advertised, especially once you stop riding hard.

The internal vest is great, and the hip valuable pocket is much better when you're all gloved up and less dextrous.

Extremely breathable (too breathable, to be honest). No chance of getting sweaty unless you get your layers very wrong.

For what it offers you can get the same warmth for a lot less outlay, and the breathability won't be too much of an issue unless you're riding hell for leather up a climb.

title: Knicks 111, Raptors 102: “Let it be 15 straight”
author: Moritz Wollert
text:
One of the more prominent flies caught in the interwebs these days was the nomination of Robert Pattinson as the new lead for the James Bond franchise. Yes, the guy who made daughters melt by the millions about two decades ago and who always looks like the vampire that made him prominent drank all the blood from his veins. Apparently he’s a really good actor, but pardon me if I’m not acting like I’m some kind of wannabe film critic just because I like movies every once in a while.

For my liking, the 007 I loved ended with the retirement of Roger Moore, a second gut punch not needed after the grim realization that Sean Connery’s time in Her Majesty’s Service was over (we ignore Roger Lazenby for obvious reasons). Before watching any of the newer films, I always much rather flopped in one of the classics, because with the world spinning faster every day, there are just some things in life I’d like to stay the way they are. Like that bank account from December before all the insurance companies wish you a happy new year or that favorite dish your Grandma used to make before she discovered light whipping cream. And while we’re at it, the fact that the New York Knicks do not lose to the Toronto Raptors.

Knicks work their late-game magic – again

After watching the Knicks almost win a carbon copy of their game on Sunday in Toronto for their 15th in a row against the Dinos, it truly feels like some divine decree puts some prehistoric panic on the Raptors in the final minutes and sprinkles just enough calmness on the orange and blue to pull it out in the end. Just like Unmitigated Gall wrote in the celebratory Postgame Thread: “Sayeth the Lord: Let it be 15 straight”. But maybe it’s also just pure and legit NBA talent taking over, and prevailing over the guys who are airballing free throws or thought it was a good idea to give Jakob Poeltl north of 100 million dollars to play basketball.

Even if Jalen Brunson shot it as purely as “The Man with the Golden Gun,” late everything for New York started and ended last night with Karl-Anthony Towns. Early in the season, he looks sharper than Oddjob’s razor-edged hat (shoutout to “Tosh Togo” Harold Sakata) and, on top of it, more powerful than Richard Kiel’s “Jaws”. KAT’s dominance was on full display against a team that could only put defenders on him who were either too small or too slow. Dismantling those adversaries wasn’t even the most impressive thing the 31-year-old did, as his passing at times was as beautiful as Honey Ryder, Tatiana Romanova and Miss Galore combined.

To be serious for a second: It is astonishing how Karl-Anthony Towns has turned around his career after more than a decade in the league. He is by far the most consistent Knick right now, has cut down on his foul issues for the time being, and looks extremely decisive on both ends of the court. In Minnesota, he always gave the impression of lacking professionalism, and now he looks like the most serious player on a team full of guys who seemingly laughed the last time the Raptors or Nets beat the Knicks. Maybe “You only live twice” as a basketball player, but in KAT’s case that looks to be plenty enough.

Karl-Anthony Towns shines for New York

The “License to Kill” in the end, of course, rests with his buddy about a foot shorter than him. You wouldn’t believe it watching the first half last night as the Raptors’ eyes got as wide seeing Jalen Brunson defend them as Auric Goldfinger’s were when he saw that shiny gold bar on the 18th green at Stoke Park. If there was a possession where Toronto didn’t attack Brunson in the first half, I seriously cannot remember it. The same goes for any offensive possession that didn’t end up with a late shot clock. It was really a desperate look at times, so desperate that Mike Brown even turned to a zone in the second half, called blitzes when Toronto barely crossed midcourt, and gave sparkplug Jose Alvarado the nod late in the third quarter. And as so often in the past, some of that stuff worked (we still do not like those traps, Mikey).

With the game on the line, the Knicks turned into a rolling “Thunderball” that just couldn’t be stopped. Mikal Bridges locked down on defense for the second straight game, the backup point guard duelists provided numerous little plays, OG Anunoby smiled, and Landry Shamet once again looked like some cool device Q designed in an underground bunker – the red button unleashes movement threes and hellish defense on the opponent. And you have to deal with KAT and Brunson on top of all that? Good luck. When the orange and blue have it going like that, it seems as if they could even make some of those megalomaniac Bond villain plots for world supremacy work. Everything seems possible – even the Captain swatting shots and turning into Jalen Dikembe Mutombo Mpolondo Mukamba Jean-Jacques Wamutombo Brunson. RIP to the legend.

Since “Diamonds Are Forever,” we really do not need a constant reminder of everything these Knicks are capable of; we still remember last year pretty well. That doesn’t mean it does not feel extremely awesome and puts a comfortable calm into a fan’s heart to see them clicking on all cylinders. It would be nice if these cylinders wouldn’t take three quarters to get going, but as long as the Knicks go home with goddess Victory, there’s nothing wrong with things the way they are. Just like there probably is nothing wrong with Robert Pattinson playing James Bond, so let us all wish him well.

And let’s hope for him he’s not a Raptors fan.

title: 'Significant for cycling in the country' – British Cycling Ventures adds backing to City of London Nocturne in a bid to expand across Britain
author: Owen Rogers
text:
British Cycling Ventures has announced a partnership with London City Nocturne organiser Koru Sports, with an eye on expanding the event to other British cities.

Held over two days on the streets of the capital’s financial district, the City of London Nocturne comprises a series of criteriums, with the men’s and women’s elite races sanctioned by the UCI as Pro Criteriums. The 2027 event will be held on Friday 11 and Saturday 12 June next year, with the bulk of the racing happening on the second day.

The partnership between organiser Koru Sports Group will aim to develop the event in the long term and accelerate the event’s commercial success, but it also provides the opportunity to expand the concept further afield.

"The venture will focus on expanding the reach of the Nocturne nationally," read a British Cycling press release. "Providing new opportunities to teams and riders, while complementing and elevating the existing domestic racing structure, including the Lloyds National Circuit Series. It will focus on enhancing fan experiences and reaching new audiences in key urban markets, while delivering a strong commercial programme for the Series."

The City of London Nocturne first appeared on the capital’s streets in 2007 under the name of the Smithfield Nocturne, running as part of a wider festival of cycling for 11 years before returning in 2026 under the ownership of Koru Sports Group.

The original event attracted riders such as Geraint Thomas, Mark Cavendish and Alex Dowsett, with Hannah and Alice Barnes both winning the women’s event, while the 2026 elite races were won by Matt Bostock (Rapha Cycling Club) and Nina Lavenu (AG Insurance-Soudal Devo).

The event is not all about top-tier racing, however, with Pro-Am team races, folding bike, penny farthing and fixed-gear races, as well as those for lower categories of competitors.

The original event was run by James Pope, who has a long history organising cycling events, including the long-running, but now defunct, Revolution track series, and now owns the Koru Sports Group, the organisation behind the revamped City of London Nocturne.

"I’ve been privileged to have been organising cycling events for over two decades in the UK and have worked closely with British Cycling during this time," Pope said in a press release.

"The plans and ambition of British Cycling Ventures present an exciting opportunity to introduce a new major city racing concept in the UK starting with the City of London Nocturne. This partnership will help us create a new world-class city event format that will be a major boost to the UK racing scene, creating a fantastic experience for riders and cycling fans."

British Cycling Ventures was launched in December 2025 as a commercial arm of the governing body, with the function of overseeing commercial growth, focusing on events across all disciplines.

"This is another significant moment in the major events vision of British Cycling Ventures, and the commercial growth of major city racing in the UK," said Managing Director Darren Henry.

"The innovation and plans for growth of the Nocturne from Koru Sports Group is significant for cycling in the country, and this joint venture brings together the best expertise in our sport to deliver huge impact through high-quality events. After hosting a brilliant event in the heart of London this year, it will continue to produce a spectacular atmosphere for riders and fans alike and make it an event not to be missed."
