title: One inspired transfer and one glaring miss – We analysed the data to see who won and lost in the women's 2025-2026 transfer market
author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
text:
With the women's peloton, the three-year promotion/relegation cycle that began this year is less important since fewer teams are competing for those WorldTour licences.

However, transfers are still crucial to maintaining or improving the team's performance, getting high-profile results in races like the Tour de France Femmes and Paris-Roubaix Femmes and keeping or attracting sponsors.

UAE Team l'IMAD ended the 2026 season as the world's number one team, just edging out FDJ United-Suez in the final days of the calendar with Maeva Squiban winning the Chrono des Nations and Elisa Longo Borghini landing on the podium at the Veneto Classic.

Of course, FDJ United-Suez had a brilliant year with Demi Vollering taking out the Tour de France and World Championships, but also had plenty of success from riders like Juliette Berthet, Célia Gery, Elise Chabbey, Evita Muzic and Ally Wollaston.

SD Worx-ProTime finished off the year as the third-best team, although it could have gone better had Lorena Wiebes not been disqualified from the Giro d'Italia due to her bike being underweight . The sprinter went on to win the green jersey in the Tour de France and two stages in addition to other WorldTour wins like In Flanders Fields and the Tour of Chongming Island.

The Laboral Kutxa-Fundacion Euskadi squad quietly led the way among the ProTeams, ending the year in 13th in the UCI Team Rankings and finishing ahead of WorldTour teams Uno-X Mobility and Picnic-PostNL.

The Spanish outfit saw Usoa Ostolaza land on the podium in the Vuelta a Burgos and take fourth overall in the Vuelta España, while other riders in the team picked up points in Continental and national championships and lower-level races throughout the year.

However, the topic here is transfers , and FDJ United-Suez made the best hire of the 2025-2026 trades by bringing on German Franziska Koch, who went on to win Paris-Roubaix Femmes.

The French team's recruitment strategy was hugely successful, giving the team a net gain of 3,753 points bringing in not only Koch but also Lauren Dickson as a neo-pro, Eva van Agt from Visma-Lease a Bike and, later in the season, mountain biker Kate Courtney.

Leaving the team were Nina Buijsman, who went on to have a solid season with Human Powered Health, and Loes Adegeest, who had good results for Lidl-Trek.

However, the addition of Koch was enormous. The German had a huge season after making the move from Picnic-PostNL, and even though she was often working to help Vollering win, Koch ended the season tenth in the UCI Individual Rankings.

UAE Team l'IMAD also came out near the top in terms of transfer gains, with Mavi Garcia coming over from Liv-AlUla-Jayco and Megan Jastrab from Picnic-PostNL, more than offsetting the loss of Sofia Bertizzolo to FDJ.

Visma-Lease a Bike also made strong gains, partially thanks to new signing Sarah Van Dam from the now-defunct Ceratizit team, ending the year fifth in the team rankings.

At the other end of the spectrum, Picnic-PostNL were gutted in the transfer market. In addition to losing Charlotte Kool to Fenix-Premier Tech in a mid-season transfer last year, and Koch to FDJ, they saw Nienke Vinke leave for SD Worx-ProTime, and Jastrab head to UAE Team l'IMAD. They dropped to 17th in the UCI Team Rankings and suffered a net loss of 4,647 points.

The Women's WorldTour is not as competitive during this cycle, with only 14 of the maximum 15 slots filled, and it's also uncertain if any of the ProTeams have the budget to apply for the WorldTour, so Picnic-PostNL may not be too concerned about their future. However, if Laboral Kutxa-Fundaction Euskadi - the top ProTeam in 13th this year - and Volkerwessels in 15th bid for WorldTour licenses, that could knock the German squad out of the WorldTour in 2029.

Franziska Koch had a massive boost from her move in 2026, ending the season as the 10th best rider in the world. The German had clearly outgrown Picnic-PostNL, where she began making major strides in 2024 and 2025. Koch got a new coach after joining FDJ United-Suez, and said she thrived in the more relaxed, professional atmosphere when interviewed by Cyclingnews during the Spring Classics .

Even while working as a valuable domestique for the world's top rider, Demi Vollering, Koch finished on the podium in Strade Bianche, and in the top 10 in the Tour of Flanders. Her main success of the year was a surprise victory in Paris-Roubaix over Marianne Vos and Pauline Ferrand-Prevot.

She also became the double German champion and ended the year with the bronze medal in the time trial at Worlds. Koch earned 3,278.67 points this year, an improvement of 2,693 over last year, making her the most valuable transfer of 2026.

Canadian Sarah van Dam was another rider who benefited greatly from a change of scenery. Her 2025 team Ceratizit went under, but Van Dam levelled up with Visma-Lease a Bike.

Van Dam showed promise last year with a podium in the Itzulia Women, and continued her upward trajectory with Visma, taking fifth in the Tour Down Under, netting stage podiums in the Tour de Suisse and Vuelta España Femenina.

She scored her first pro win in the late season at the Finistère Ladies Classic, and ended the season with podiums in the Giro dell'Emilia and Tre Valli Varesine.

Lauren Dickson (FDJ United-Suez) was the third-highest scoring of the women transfers and the top neo-pro, winning the mountains classification at the Tour of Britain, a stage of the Faun Tour Femmes, and taking third in the Giro dell'Emilia along with strong stage results in Itzulia, the Giro d'Italia and Vuelta a Extremadura.

The next-best neo-pro was Australian champion Mackenzie Coupland, who graduated from Liv's development team to the WorldTour Liv-AlUla-Jayco squad and scored top results in the Cadel Evans Great Ocean Road Race, won the Vuelta a Extremadura, and finished fifth in the under-23 time trial at Worlds.

Another notable new rider was Sandrine Tas, the former speed skater who signed with Lotto-Intermarché. She won two stages of the Bretagne Ladies Tour and finished second overall, then ended the year with a stage win in the Eneco Tour, too.

The women's statistics tell an interesting story: Canyon-SRAM and Movistar scored all of their points with returning riders, which didn't happen in the men's teams. In the graph above their bubble size is miniscule, reflecting the fact that zero percent of the team's points came from incoming riders.

As a percentage of their massive points, transfers didn't have as outsized of an impact on the top teams' rankings, but at the other end of the spectrum, incoming riders made a big difference for smaller teams.

Lotto-Intermarché profited from the addition of speedskater Sandrine Tas, who quickly became a formidable sprinter with wins in the Bretagne Ladies Tour and Eneco Tour and a podium in the GP Stuttgart.

Together, the team climbed nine places into 19th overall with 64.5% of their points coming from Tas and Linda Riedmann, winner of Binche-Chimay-Binche.

St Michel-Preference Home-Auber93 made a bold move to sign former Paris-Roubaix winner Alison Jackson as part of a near-total revamp of their roster, with only four riders returning. They climbed up four places into 22nd.

Transfers didn't work out quite as well for teams like Liv-AlUla-Jayco, who dropped three spots into 11th after losing Mavi Garcia to UAE, and Lidl-Trek, who dropped from fourth to sixth place after losing Lizzie Deignan and Ellen van Dijk to retirement and not finding riders of the same level to replace them.

Because the women's teams can only score half of their maximum roster size, unlike the men's teams, where non-scored riders made next to no difference in their ranking of all riders' totals vs. the UCI Team Rankings, there were some significant differences for women.

The total number of points scored by riders not making the top 10 of their team signals depth in the roster.

UAE Team l'IMAD had the highest total points that didn't factor into their team rankings with 3,037. Of the transfers, Jastrab, with 646 and a top 10 in Paris-Roubaix, was among those not counting toward the team's total. Federica Venturelli (490 points) from the development squad was also a strong addition to UAE Team l'IMAD's depth.

FDJ United-SUEZ seriously padded their roster, and in addition to Koch and Dickson's fine seasons, they brought on Evan van Agt and Kate Courtney, each of whom earned more than 300 points that weren't counted toward the team's rankings.

Lidl-Trek, too, have great depth - their bottom ten riders scored 2,966 points - more than Picnic-PostNL's entire team! While most of that depth came from returning riders, incoming transfers Margot Vanpachtenbeke and Ricarda Bauernfeind scored over 300 points each that weren't part of the ranking total.

AG Insurance-Soudal added to their depth, with a significant percentage of their total points not counting toward the UCI Team Rankings. While most of the uncounted points came from Gladys Verhulst, new hire Tess Moerman brought in 175 points that aren't reflected in their tally.

There were very few transfer misses in the women's peloton, and the incoming riders who did not perform as they had in 2025 had very good reasons. Rooijakkers was down 623 points because she went on maternity leave after only a few racing days, while Dilyxine Miermont didn't perform for Picnic-PostNL after a strong year with Ceratizit in 2025 because of a bad crash in training.

The main miss in the women's transfer market ahead of 2026 was Picnic-PostNL failing to retain their top talent or replace them with similar riders.

They lost Koch, Vinke, and Jastrab, all riders who had brilliant 2026 seasons on other teams, which is quite concerning for the team's future.

While returning riders Georgi and Nelson improved over 2025 and brought in 782 and 748 points, respectively, new hires Mia Griffin and Audrey De Keersmaeker scored only around 100 points. Six of their incoming riders scored fewer than 75 points, and most underperformed compared with last season.

Another team that had a worrying transfer performance was EF Education-Oatly, who lost Alison Jackson and Letizia Borghesi. The Italian scored 920 points for AG Insurance-Soudal through top finishes in the Trofeo Alfredo Binda, Antwerp Port Epic and the Bretagne Ladies Tour, where she finished third overall. Jackson scored 422 points in a consistent but winless season for Auber 93.

EF Education-Oatly's top transfer was Alice Towers with 244 points and a podium in Durango-Durango, but sprinter Alexis Magner was never able to reach her previous level after her horrific crash in 2025 and opted to retire at the end of the season.

Next up, once the 2027 rosters are confirmed, we will see who stands to gain the most from the 2026-2027 transfer season for both men and women.

One small note on the data: the UCI Team Rankings and the totals shown here may differ slightly because teams were given small penalties during the season. The difference was not enough to affect any of the conclusions.

title: Gent Six opening night drawn to a close early after heavy crash involving Jasper De Buyst
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
The opening night of the Gent Six track meet was stopped early on Tuesday after a major crash involving Jasper De Buyst and Jules Hesters during the final event.

32-year-old De Buyst, in his final race before retiring, will now leave the sport earlier than planned after being taken to hospital following the crash. The Belgian underwent treatment on the track for several minutes before being taken away on a stretcher.

De Buyst's Lotto-Intermarché team confirmed to that he has sustained a fractured collarbone in the fall and spent Tuesday night in the intensive care unit after a scan revealed internal bleeding around his spleen.

Following the crash, which happened with three minutes and 50 laps remaining in the team pursuit event in the famous 't Kuipke velodrome, organisers consulted with the riders and decided not to restart.

Lindsay De Vylder and Fabio Van Den Bossche hold the overall lead with 55 points, while Robbe Ghys and Yoeri Havik sit second on 41 points. Other notable competitors at the men's Gent Six include Tim Torn Teutenberg, Benjamin Thomas, and Bryan Coquard. Lotte Kopecky and Hélène Hesters headline the Ladies Cup on Friday.

De Buyst called time on his 14-year road career this year, and will take on a new role at Lotto-Intermarché as performance manager. The Gent Six was set to be his farewell to racing.

"If I can finish with a good feeling, give my maximum, and above all have fun, then I will be a happy man on Sunday," he told earlier this week.

"The podium is the ambition again this year, although unlike in previous years, I am trying not to fixate on that. Of course, I dream of finishing the way it started: with a victory, but 13 years later. But then again, I can accept it if that doesn't happen.

"I have always had a special connection with Ghent. It is a kind of 'full circle' moment to say goodbye in Ghent. I will run into friends, family, former coaches, and current coaches during the week. It provides the opportunity to see everyone who helped build even the smallest part of your career."

While De Buyst's time at the Gent Six and his racing career are now over, it doesn't mean that his partner Hesters also has to quit the race.

Wednesday night's events are individual competitions, meaning Hesters can continue to compete while he looks for a new partner for the remaining days. Gent Six regulations stipulate that he'd have to leave the competition if he doesn't find a new partner within 48 hours.

title: Former Spain midfielder Mata retires aged 38
text:
Former Spain midfielder Juan Mata has announced his retirement from playing at the age of 38.

Mata, who made 41 international appearances, was part of the Spain squad that won the 2010 World Cup, and he helped his country win the European Championship two years later when he scored in the 4-0 final victory against Italy.

A former Real Madrid youth player, he joined Valencia in 2007 before a move to Chelsea in August 2011 where he won the Champions League, Europa League and FA Cup.

Mata moved to Manchester United in January 2014 and helped them claim the Europa League, FA Cup and League Cup prior to his departure in 2022.

He went on to have spells at Turkish side Galatasaray and Vissel Kobe in Japan before he played for Australian sides Western Sydney Wanderers and Melbourne Victory.

"Football will never leave my life," said Mata. "There are so many ways to continue loving the game, so many ways to keep using it as a vehicle for development.

"I may stop playing professionally, but I will never stop being a footballer."

Mata was Chelsea's player of the year in both full seasons he was at Stamford Bridge. He made 82 league appearances for the club, scoring 18 goals.

"What a player," Chelsea posted on social media.

At Manchester United, he scored 51 goals in 285 outings before leaving after his contract expired.

"Congratulations on a fantastic career, Juan! Everyone at United wishes you all the best in your next steps," said United statement. , external

Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling
author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
text:
A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza

Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay , if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.

The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.

It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.

The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.

The US and Israel fear the final judgment may clarify how to establish a government’s intent to commit a genocide, and so set a precedent that makes it more likely the court will later rule that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.

Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents.

The ICJ, sometimes described as the UN’s top court, is responsible for settling interstate disputes, unlike the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes.

The US has already imposed crippling sanctions on judges at the ICC after the court issued arrest warrants against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The US has also announced sanctions against the entire ICC as an institution, which it described as a “rogue court”. Washington fears the ICC could go after US troops.

The Gambia, as a litigant, was entitled to appoint an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar and chose the South African lawyer Pillay, who in October was awarded the Nobel peace prize . She is required to act as a jurist and not an advocate for the Gambia.

Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, has sent a warning shot to Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges, saying Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops”.

Waltz asserted last month: “The ICJ ad hoc judge Navi Pillay is tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar, intending to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians.”

In remarks addressed to Pillay, he said: “We see your agenda and we’ll be watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely.”

In a speech last Friday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio , said: “For this global elite, international law … is an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles.”

He warned the ICC against quoting laws to “men with swords”.

Israel has previously criticised adverse advisory opinions issued by the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring Israel to admit more aid into Gaza , and to cooperate with Unrwa, the UN relief and works agency.

In the Myanmar case, a 24-page submission jointly filed by the UK and five other mainly European states, argued that the ICJ, in judging intent to commit genocide, should examine a range of “facts and circumstances” assessed “comprehensively and holistically”.

It also stressed that genocide was not solely defined by killings, and that the treatment of children, gender-based violence and forced displacement were also relevant.

The US until recently had taken a relatively more benign view of The Hague-based ICJ, and under Antony Blinken as US secretary of state determined that Myanmar had committed genocide.

The 15 ICJ judges are elected for nine-year terms by the UN security council and the UN general assembly.

Rubio has given the ICC until April to respond to his criticisms before he imposes sanctions.

On Friday, the ICC formally decided to drop plans to prosecute US soldiers and intelligence agents for potentially unlawful acts in Afghanistan. The shelving of the near-dormant inquiry came after it was agreed evidence would be hard to obtain, but one side-effect may be a greater willingness on the part of the US to abandon its plan to impose sanctions on the ICC.

text:
Mauricio Pochettino has said he will restore Manchester United to being the most successful footballing side in the city.

The Argentine is scheduled to begin his new role as United manager on Wednesday after agreeing a two-and-a-half-year contract.

The United States beat Haiti 2-0 in Cincinnati in his final game in charge on Tuesday, after which he spoke to TNT Sports. , external

"Leaving is tough at this moment, but sometimes in football an opportunity comes that is impossible to say no to. I have always believed in following my heart, even when it means leaving a place where I have been very happy.

title: Cowboy boots, cocktails and casinos - how do three US grands prix compare?
text:
"The picnic blanket that you'd happily sit on in Austin will get confiscated by security at Miami and will end up wrapped around you in the chill of a Vegas night."

Cadence Kim from Dallas lives the reality of being an avid Formula 1 fan in the United States, in the three diverse locations the sport now frequents. She will be among the 300,000 spectators around the iconic Las Vegas Strip this weekend.

Las Vegas joined the F1 calendar in 2023, a year after Miami, while Austin has been home to the United States Grand Prix since 2012.

Kim has put in the hard yards travelling across the Atlantic to witness F1 in its European heartland. Now she is reaping the rewards of owners Liberty Media investing heavily in the three US races, which have all recently been awarded new long-term contracts.

"Following F1 from the US used to mean accepting a massive barrier to entry," Kim explains.

"It meant setting an early alarm and trying to explain to room mates why you were yelling at 20 rich men driving funny-looking cars very quickly. It was more of a niche sport with no natural gathering places for a community to watch. What bar is open at that time?

"Having three domestic races has changed everything. It has shifted F1 from a purely broadcast experience into something tangible. It becomes a week-long experience where a fan gets to engage with a like-minded community, attend parties in the evening, and do a meet-and-greet. You can walk a track, sit in a grandstand, purchase the overpriced merch, hear the engines and literally feel a part of something."

The community Kim is attached to is the ATX GP Club, formed in Austin by Maria Rodriguez and Julia Wezio, where watch parties help fans learn more about the sport and the drivers. With the longest running of the US races on their doorstep, at the Circuit of the Americas, she's ideally placed to compare all three venues for the fan experience.

"Vegas is a party," exclaims Kim. "The Nevada desert gets cold at night, so the cowboy hat doesn't make the trip, but socks, a hoodie and gloves do.

"Many of the teams have hotel partnerships so lobbies become team activation zones, and you might end up sharing an elevator with an engineer. The fan flow is well managed with everyone being funnelled through specific pedestrian walkways, but if you do have a ticket to watch the race at the track you are limited to staying only in that one specific zone.

"Vegas is known for its dining but that doesn't make it to the track. Ticketing forces you to consider some pretty rigid trade-offs. For example, sitting at Turn One means missing the musical artists and activations by the Sphere.

"As for Austin, you aren't restricted to a single assigned area but can walk almost the entire perimeter of the track. With each of the three races you get a local vibe integrated into the entertainment. It's not an artificially manufactured aesthetic in Austin, you're getting real Texas BBQ, smoked brisket and bedazzled cowboy hats.

"I've been once to Miami and would not consider going back unless it became a night race. The South Florida sun bakes both the track and the attendees during the daytime. Preparing for an outdoor trek is the best mindset. Treat it like a multi-day hike where you'll be logging 30,000 steps each day so comfortable shoes and water with electrolyte packets are a must."

The excitement level of racing at the Las Vegas Grand Prix in its opening three years has been as bright as the neon lights on the Strip. The debut race in 2023 was an instant classic, with the lead changing hands five times, and drama all the way to the line as Charles Leclerc overtook Sergio Perez for second place, behind winner Max Verstappen.

It was instant payback for F1, who had invested more than £500m in buying land and promoting the event. Despite complaints from some local residents and businesses over the disruption to the city streets, the gamble has paid dividends, according to Vegas-based podcast host and nine-time Le Mans 24 Hours driver Justin Bell.

"I was telling people, 'just wait'. It's like a big piece of Ikea furniture – once you do it once, it's so much quicker and more efficient the next time," Bell tells BBC Sport.

"The promoters did listen to the locals and worked out ways to get them involved, by offering discounted tickets and attempting to minimise the disruption. Let's face it, Las Vegas exists for one reason and that is to entertain visitors, and with the extraordinary economic impact it has I am sure the pros outweigh the cons for almost everyone involved."

That economic impact has been valued at $3.2bn for the Southern Nevada region over the three years, with each of the 175,000 visitors from outside Las Vegas spending an average of $2,400 on non-racing activities, according to figures from the 2024 race.

Bell, who presents the Drive to Wynn podcast from the luxury resort on the Strip, and used to guide celebrities like Drew Barrymore and Steve Carell in race cars on the Jay Leno Show, thinks Vegas has the perfect opportunity to position itself as the premier US race, despite it being the youngest.

"Vegas has such a leg up on the other two locations as a global entertainment hub, that aligns so well with the direction that F1 is heading as a brand," he says. "Miami is sexy and in theory has much going for it, but the track itself isn't in Miami so there are the usual inconveniences in terms of transportation.

"In contrast, I always recommended Austin to F1 newcomers as a track to visit first, because it is a purpose-built facility that is so easy to spectate at, with tons of room to walk around and watch cars from every angle all while eating a hotdog.

"From the first laps from 2023, it became evident that the Vegas track design was going to be great for F1. The mix of tight corners with that long straight down the iconic Strip invites breathtaking overtaking. Each successive year gets better."…

title: How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?
text:
Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom.

No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.

That partnership has now ended following Huang's resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, one of which is alleged to have been with a Chinese spy.

The company has been rocked by the scandal, with hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value and questions swirling about the extent of the impact of Huang's departure.

While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.

The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.

Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.

It is now one the most valuable firms, worth $3.8 trillion (£2.9 trillion), and on Tuesday said its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier.

But there's now an air of uncertainty over Nvidia's future direction. Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on the company, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him.

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at investment firm AJ Bell, says because Huang was also a key figure in "flying the flag" to drum up enthusiasm and investment for the wider AI industry, his departure posed a "real risk" that Nvidia could now decide to change its current strategy and rein in spending.

Such a move could spell a wider slowdown in AI investment, which would have an economic impact. How big? That's "unknown", Coatsworth says.

"If they decide to go with the much more cautious route... there could be a knock-on effect in that you have got various companies in the AI infrastructure space suddenly finding they don't have a key source of finance," he says.

Kunjan Sobhani, senior technology industry analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, expects the impact of Huang leaving to be "limited" for now as Nvidia has strong commitments and a deep order book. But he said this picture could change in the long run.

That is because Nvidia, on its journey to the top of the AI industry, has created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing".

Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly.

The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy?

That risk is perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, have called for Huang's reinstatement.

Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, which has also prompted a campaign by shareholders and supporters to "Bring Jensen Back".

Huang himself has said he is open to a return, just days after resigning .

Coatsworth says he has never seen circular financing used at this scale before, but admits there are competitive rivals around, which could insulate the wider AI industry from any potential slowdown at the firm.

When Nvidia's share price plunged in the wake of the affair revelations, the stock of its rival semiconductor makers including AMD, Broadcom and Marvell Technology jumped.

"I don't think all AI activity grinds to a halt if Nvidia slows down what it's doing and if it pulls some financing, but it does change how people would look at the whole situation," Coatsworth adds.

The risk of a slowdown has already rattled stock markets. Investors took fright at Democrat gains in the midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms.

Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will actually pay off.

Investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, who said the technology would remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.

Nvidia's interim boss Colette Kress said it was "business as usual" without Huang at the helm as the company's rapid growth remains on track.

The value of the shares in Big Tech companies have cushioned the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs, buoying investments and pensions for people worldwide.

Despite Huang saying he would be "honoured" to return, Nvidia's board has said it is not considering bringing him back.

And while Coatsworth thinks "no CEO is irreplaceable", he admits the pressure is on for whoever succeeds him.

title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt
author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
text:
Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans

The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.

The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen , the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.

The disclosure raises broader questions about the EU-Egypt relationship, as Egyptian authorities face scrutiny over shrinking press freedom following the jailing and alleged torture of six journalists , the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, a factchecking and investigative platform, and the closure last month of one of the country’s last independent news outlets and conviction of its high-profile editor , Lina Attalah.

Attalah is appealing against that conviction and will be in court this week as she seeks to overturn other charges including “publishing false news” , for which she was sentenced to a year in prison in absentia without her knowledge.

The spotlight is on €5bn in EU “soft” loans to Egypt – lending with easy repayment terms, known as macro-financial assistance, that is meant to be available only to countries that respect human rights and democracy. While the EU conditions on democracy and rights are vague, the loans impose much more specific requirements on Egypt to carry out economic reforms.

Separate data sources – from leaked EU documents and deleted from an Egyptian government website – raise questions about the European Commission’s claims that Egypt met targets linked to social welfare programmes, which enabled the EU to release €2.5bn in assistance.

In confidential documents, the commission told EU lawmakers that Egypt had “broadly fulfilled” and then “fulfilled” two separate targets to increase the numbers of poor people on social welfare programmes between 2024 and 2026. But data points to a net reduction of 85,734 households as the Egyptian government removed people from its welfare programmes rather than expanded coverage.

If Egypt had expanded the programmes in line with the EU’s apparent conditions – and not removed any households – about 245,000 households, equivalent to roughly 909,000 people, would be getting these benefits. (The Guardian used World Bank data to make this rough calculation).

According to the leaked documents, the commission wanted Egypt to “further expand cash transfer programmes”, but despite a net reduction in beneficiaries it gave the green light anyway to two separate “soft” loans totalling €2.5bn.

In response to the Guardian’s findings, one of the European parliament’s leading spokespeople on EU-Egypt relations, the Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, said she was introducing a question to the European Commission demanding clarification.

“The finding by this investigation that the commission is seemingly sugarcoating Egypt’s performance is worrying,” Strik said. “From the beginning, the commission has used macro-financial assistance primarily as a tool to lure Egypt into migration cooperation, while considering formal conditions and its reporting obligations towards parliament as an inconvenient formality.”

Under the plan, Egypt has so far received €3.5bn in soft loans in three instalments, with a final payment of €1.5bn expected before the end of 2027.

The charge of sugarcoating figures relates to two social welfare programmes: the Takaful and Karama cash transfer programmes for poor and vulnerable households.

The Takaful (Solidarity) programme gives poor families cash payments as long as recipients have regular health visits and good attendance at school. The Karama (Dignity) programme gives unconditional cash payments to people living with a disability, older people, orphans and widows.

One of the EU conditions for Egypt to gain the first €1bn loan was to increase the number of Takaful and Karama beneficiary households by 100,000 to 4.7 million.

In a leaked report to lawmakers in the EU council of ministers and the European parliament, the commission described that requirement as “broadly fulfilled”.

The data in that report, however, reveals a net fall of 62,281 households during this period, owing to what the EU officials describe as “a multi-annual recertification process”. Some beneficiaries were added to the list but a larger number were removed because they were deemed ineligible.

In order to achieve a later instalment of €1.5bn, Egypt was required to “further expand” the programmes, adding 60,000 households to the Takaful and Karama beneficiaries list. A second leaked report to EU lawmakers shows that the commission concluded the target was “fulfilled” because 442,118 families were added to the list.

On this occasion, the commission did not report on numbers removed. Figures from Egypt’s ministry of social solidarity, however, show a net reduction of 23,453 beneficiaries to the programmes in the 11 months until June 2026, the period leading up to the release of that payment. The EU announced the release of the €1.5bn payment in July 2026.

The data has since been deleted from the Egyptian ministry website but the Guardian has seen screenshots and archived webpages.

During a period from 2024 to 26 when the EU required Egypt to add 160,000 households to the rolls of the Karama and Takaful programmes, there was a net decline of 85,734 households.…

title: Jeff Bezos says he was 'heavily involved' in casting Robert Pattinson as new Bond
text:
Jeff Bezos has said he was "heavily involved" in casting Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond.

Speaking at an event in California, the Amazon CEO said he was originally "biased against" Pattinson - who starred in many blockbuster films like Batman and the Twilight series - "because he's already so famous".

The role of 007 has typically gone to an actor who is not as well known at the time of casting. But Bezos said in screen tests, "it was so obvious he is James Bond".

This will be the first 007 film in the official series not under the creative control of the Broccoli family, who had overseen the franchise since the first movie in 1962. Amazon purchased MGM, which co-owns the franchise, in 2022.

Robert Pattinson: How the Twilight star became 007

'Good Bond vibes' - Hollywood locals react to Robert Pattinson cast as new 007

"There was something special about Rob", Bezos said at Semafor Silicon Valley & The World Event on Tuesday.

Pattinson was unveiled as the franchise's seventh James Bond on Monday, taking over from actor Daniel Craig. He will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028.

In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime."

The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.

The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment.

Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks.

But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands.

"We ran a really tight process and made the final decision on Friday," Bezos said.

There were five finalists who went through "real, old-fashioned screen tests", acting out three different scenes in full costume, with real sets and other actors, he said.

"By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance," Bezos added. "It was immediately un-debated. Denis [Villeneuve], the director … we all gravitated toward Rob."

The pick comes amid widespread Hollywood cuts and consolidation, with studios struggling to get people into cinemas.

Hollywood insiders have said Pattinson was viewed as a safe pick to bring audiences in, rather than taking a risk on a new actor who could grow with the franchise.

"Maybe he's boring. Maybe Hollywood would be passing up a chance to anoint a badly needed new star. But with so much at stake for everyone involved, that all makes him the obvious pick," Hollywood journalist Matthew Belloni, who predicted the pick, wrote in his newsletter.

The BBC's Regan Morris contributed to this report.

title: Why SBT GRVL Is Challenging Another Race Over Four Letters
author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
text:
SBT GRVL has been embroiled in online controversy after an uproar over the brand’s enforcement of a trademark around the term GRVL.

It all started with an Instagram post. @rezgravel on Instagram, the page representing an Indigenous-led community gravel event in Sacaton, Arizona, posted an email they received from SBT GRVL requesting that Rez Gravel stop using the term GRVL in marketing materials around the event.

The Rez Gravel post was a protest of that email. The post comment highlighted the lack of infrastructure around the Rez Gravel event, how the email from SBT would force them to spend money they don’t have on new posters and a logo redesign, and criticism of the lack of care and consideration SBT GRVL showed in denying their request for comped entry into SBT GRVL for native riders in the past.

That post generated over a thousand likes and hundreds of comments, with many people criticizing SBT GRVL, bringing into question the viability of a trademark of the term GRVL, and supporting the Indigenous-led event and organization.

On Sunday, November 15th, Rez Gravel posted a screenshot of an email the race received from SBT GRVL around the use of the GRVL term on previous marketing material for their January 9th and 10th community bike rides.

“So I guess @sbtgrvl owns ‘GRVL’ and we’ll have to stop using GRVL,” the caption under Rez Gravel’s post read. “SBT GRVL introduced me to gravel cycling when I was an @rideforracialjustice RFRJ athlete in 2022. In the past, I have been one of SBT GRVL’s biggest supporters. I returned to SBT GRVL in 2023, 2024 and in 2023 even went halfway around the world to support their race @fnldgrvl FNLD GRVL in Finland.

“I tried to bring a Native Gravel team to SBT GRVL in 2024. I tried to ask Amy, Ryan, and Greer for free or even discounted entry as a way to honor the First Nations people, including my cousin from the Ute Indian Tribe- Uintah and Ouray Reservation, whose people were removed from the land in the area now known as Steamboat Springs. Amy and her team refused to honor native people with even a reduced-fee entry for my cousin in 2024.”

And then came the crux of their argument.

“Rez Gravel does not use the GRVL in our LLC, DBA, or website names. Rez Gravel does not sell any merchandise that uses the GRVL name or logo. Rez Gravel is owned by a Gila River Indian Community tribal member and solely operates on the Gila River Indian Community a Sovereign Nation.

“Rez Gravel only has an annual revenue of around $4,000, and after expenses only about 2,000-3,000 keeps our community bike shop going for the year. The posters are printed for 2027 and out of money until some more funds come in from 2027 Registration.”

A second post from the Rez Gravel organization a day later added to that online discourse, with the organization posting details of the federally registered trademarks that SBT GRVL invoked in their emails and a caption that articulated how the Rez Gravel organization was not infringing upon the two separate trademarks that SBT GRVL has around the term GRVL.

In total, SBT GRVL has trademarks on the terms SBT GRVL, FNLD GRVL, RADL GRVL, and two specific trademarks around the term GRVL. One of those terms covers cycling events, while the other protects the use of GRVL for merchandise.

In the case of Rez Gravel, SBT GRVL didn’t specify which trademark they were invoking—they did not have to since the email was a courtesy note and not a formal cease—but it is likely the trademark around the event.

In an exclusive interview with Velo , the SBT GRVL organizers explained the reason behind the email and their trademarks.

“It was back a few years ago that we decided that we needed to trademark the event,” Amy Charity, the SBT GRVL race director, told Velo.

“We had established a brand, and we knew that SBT GRVL stood for something that we were really proud of. We were a safe event, an event that was inclusive, an event that was credible and professional.

“At the time, we were also considering expanding our brand by putting on events such as FNLND GRVL or RADL GRVL. In doing so, we wanted to ensure that the riders, the participants, and the sponsors would know what they were getting—when you hear GRVL, when you see GRVL, there’s a standard that you associate with what we will uphold and what we’ll honor.”

Like all trademark processes, that trademark process took many months to complete with the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO). In that process, to get the trademarks for the term GRVL, SBT GRVL had to both prove distinctiveness and prove they were using the trademark to identify their brand to consumers.

Additionally, as with all trademark or copyright instances, SBT GRVL had to demonstrate they were actively using the trademark for commercial use, and that they are actively enforcing their intellectual property if they deem that trademark has been violated.

That has meant that each time an event has used the GRVL distinction since, they have been required by law to notify the brand that is using their trademarked term.

“The very first time it happened, it was because there was confusion in the marketplace,” Ryan Steers, SBT GRVL’s Marketing Director, told Velo. “We had a sponsor approach us and say, we didn’t know that you were putting on an event in a different country, and asked why we didn’t tell them we were doing it and why they weren’t the first that you approached.

“It was confusing, especially in our market, particularly because it was a US-based company putting on an international event with GRVL in the title. So we reached out to that event business and said, ‘Hey, we wanted to give you a heads-up, we own the trademark for GRVL as it relates to events.’

“That’s what we do when we see an event out there related to gravel cycling that has been using GRVL. There have been around three events that we’ve reached out to.”…

title: Can Labour end the youth unemployment crisis? – podcast
author: Presented by Nosheen Iqbal; produced by George McDonagh, Ivor Manley , Harriet Mogie and Rudi Zygadlo; executive producer Eli Block
text:
There are about a million young people across the country not in employment, education or training. Could Alan Milburn’s landmark report help change that? Richard Partington reports

The UK has one of the worst rates in Europe when it comes to youth unemployment. From the savage cuts to youth services during austerity, to the impacts of the pandemic and now the threat of AI to entry level jobs, young people across the country are feeling that the social contract is broken.

But now Alan Milburn, the 68-year-old New Labour veteran, has published a radical review urging the government to spend billions on a new deal for young people.

However, it comes at a price. Because at the same time, Milburn is proposing massive changes to the welfare system, with cuts specifically designed to hit those under 25.

The answer must be radical, he says. “This cannot be fixed by tweaking the edges of the existing system. The response now has to be full throttle: not another initiative or another round of incremental reform, but transformational change.”

title: Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as it reports soaring sales
text:
Nvidia's quarterly sales doubled to top $100bn for the first time as the company insisted it has no plans to reinstate ousted co-founder Jensen Huang.

In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit , interim chief executive Colette Kress said it is "business as usual" and told investors: "We've got this."

The company's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier, reaching $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading.

Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China.

"The board does not intend to reinstate him," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said during a call on Tuesday with financial analysts.

The company's profits also doubled from a year ago. For the quarter, which covered the three months to 25 October, profit hit $65bn. Its revenue from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn in the same period.

Going forward, the company said its rapid growth is poised to continue, and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter.

Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure that Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worries that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader.

"The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."

Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout that is happening throughout the technology industry.

"It is business as usual," she said. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."

She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects".

"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."

The interim CEO also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre semiconductors to China.

The Hopper technology is in Nvidia's advanced H200 processors, which the firm won approval to sell in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.

They had previously been restricted over concerns that selling them to China would give its industries and military an edge over the US.

Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments had been stopped.

The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal

Jensen Huang says he would be 'honoured' to return as Nvidia CEO if board asked him

Despite board chairman Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analysts' questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement.

He said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection.

"With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new CEO will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person."

Michael Monaghan from investment firm Founder ETFs is among those who want Huang back in the top job at Nvidia.

The Nvidia investor told the BBC that he is waiting to see the results of a thorough investigation into Huang's actions, instead of relying on "salacious allegations" made in the media.

Nvidia's strong earnings are "from the machine that Jensen built" and a company tends to lose "its shine and vision" after an iconic founder leaves, Monaghan said.

title: A potato war has been simmering for decades between the US and Japan. It’s about to reach boiling point
author: Justin McCurry in Tokyo
text:
Under pressure from Donald Trump, Japan’s government could be about to lift a ban on imported American potatoes, which famers say would threaten their livelihoods

It could be a piping hot croquette eaten on the go, a bowl of nikujaga stew or a plate of home-cooked chips. One culinary thread runs through them all – the Japanese potato.

Along with rice , the crop is fiercely protected as one of only a few homegrown staples in a country that imports more than 60% of its food.

But that could be about to change. Under pressure from Donald Trump , Japan is moving towards lifting a 76-year-old ban on imported American potatoes .

Japan’s potato farmers say lifting the ban would threaten their livelihoods, and expose consumers to an inferior product. They worry batches of American potatoes could bring harmful insects and pests into Japanese fields.

Tokyo partially lifted the ban in 2006 to permit imports of US potatoes exclusively to make crisps. The vegetables must be transported in sealed containers and then cooked at a high temperature to prevent the spread of pests and diseases.

But a complete lifting of the ban would put fresh American potatoes on restaurant menus and supermarket shelves for the first time since 1950.

“We have repeatedly and unequivocally stated our opposition to imports,” said Toshihide Numasawa, an employee of the Japan Agriculture group in Hokkaido, where about 80% of the country’s potatoes are grown. He said there were various reasons for the objection, including the “risk of pests and diseases entering the country and damage to Hokkaido’s production areas.”

Potatoes were initially collector’s items for intrigued plant enthusiasts when Dutch traders introduced them to Japan in 1598. By the mid-1800s, potatoes were a nutritious alternative to rice – a crop unsuited to Hokkaido’s cooler climate. Now they are the basis for the perennial favourite jaga bata , a baked version slathered in butter, while poteto sarada has practically achieved national-dish status.

Hokkaido’s best-known variety is the Danshaku (Irish Cobbler), a potato high in starch whose fluffy, absorbent flesh makes them perfect for butter and other toppings or to soak up meat juices in a stew.

“We believe consumers have come to recognise which are best suited to particular dishes,” said Numasawa, adding that Hokkaido potato farmers were also being buffeted by homegrown pest outbreaks, global heating and rural depopulation.

The country now grows more than 90 varieties of potato and Japanese consumers ate 3.5m tons of potatoes in 2024, according to the agriculture ministry, among them 1.2m tons of fresh imports used to make crisps.

The tuber’s place at the centre of Japan-US trade negotiations has created an early headache for Japan’s new agriculture minister, Arata Takebe, whose constituency is located in prime potato-growing country in Hokkaido.

The plan to lift the ban “should progress after thorough scientific and technical discussion” Takebe recently told Jiji Press, adding that a decision could take “considerable time”.

“I know the [US] side has strong expectations, but the ban on imports will not be lifted without sufficient discussions or an agreement acceptable to both sides,” he said.

While potatoes imported for crisps are subject to strict quarantine measures, farmers fear batches of imported fresh potatoes could bring in harmful insects and microbes. Japan’s government has identified 21 pests and diseases that could pose a risk of invasion.

The potato cyst nematode and pale potato cyst nematode are causing most concern. Although they are not a threat to human health, they can damage the vegetable’s roots, which stunts their growth, and remain present in soil for more than 15 years.

Earlier this year, congressional lawmakers urged Trump to continue raising the ban with the Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi.

“US potato growers produce the best potatoes in the world,” they wrote in a letter. “Japan represents a massive market with significant export opportunities for American potato growers.”

After raising the issue during his first term in office, Trump has persuaded Japan’s government to begin talks as he faces accusations that his policies have been “ disastrous ” for rural America.

Supporters of lifting the ban say it would lower prices for Japanese consumers and bring American farmers an additional $150m a year in export earnings.

But farmers in Hokkaido claim that not enough has been done to eliminate the threat from pests and disease.

“Protecting Hokkaido’s agriculture is not just about protecting Hokkaido,” the Hokkaido Agricultural Corporations Association said in a statement. “It also means protecting the production base that will support Japan’s food supply for the future.”

Naohiro Makino, a potato farmer in Hokkaido, said the ban on fresh potatoes should stay. “Once pests get in, you can’t grow potatoes for more than a decade,” he told the Asahi Shimbun newspaper. “For the sake of the farmland our ancestors protected, I am firmly opposed [to lifting the ban].”

title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave
text:
"Photonic chips are on the verge of a breakthrough," says Ton van Mol of the Dutch research institute TNO.

If van Mol is right – and TNO, the European Union and the Dutch government are backing the idea with millions of euros - then the technology could be a gamechanger.

The chips which run today's society, from your phone and TV, to the vast data centres meeting our insatiable desire for AI, are mostly electrical.

They process data by shunting electrons around tiny circuits – a single microchip produced today can contain billions of transistors, and sizes are measured in nanometres (one nanometre is a billionth of a metre).

Because they use light instead of electricity, photonic chips are faster, use less energy and generate less heat than traditional computer chips.

Van Mol hopes for an acceleration in photonics similar to the one seen in electrical chips since the 1970s.

"With optical chips, you are now where electronic chips were maybe 40 [or] 50 years ago."

American, Taiwanese and Chinese firms dominate the computer chip industry, but Europe sees the emergence of photonic chips as a fresh opportunity to lead, on what could be, a key future technology.

Which is why the European Union has committed €400m ($450m; £330m) to a project called PIX Europe , external , with the stated goal of making the continent "a global leader in emerging technology for Photonic Integrated Chips".

"Europe said 'we need to have our own manufacturing in-house'," says van Mol, who is leading a key part of the programme.

"We cannot depend like in the past that everything is manufactured in the US or China - that's not wise, so the [European] Chips Act was called into life, and one of the parts of the act is to build pilot lines to really bring the technology, which is now in labs, to the next stage - manufacturing."

Electronic and photonic chips are produced on wafers made up of hundreds of individual chips. Factories with machines that can handle bigger wafers can churn out chips more efficiently.

"[Photonic chip] manufacturing worldwide is [currently] done on wafers which are four inches (10cm) in size, and the next step is to scale-up production to a six-inch wafer," says van Mol.

His team are already building a 10,000 sq m factory to produce six-inch indium phosphide wafers on the High Tech Campus in the Dutch city of Eindhoven.

It's due to fully open in 2030 and will be a major step forward, not just for photonics in Europe, but around the world, according to van Mol.

"That's the development TNO is going to do, in a pilot line which is really serious.

"In 2030, we hope that we have a stable, reproducible, high-yield process, and then the intention is that the pilot line [opens] to industrial parties who can make commercial production out of it."

Europe does have one crucial player in the current computer chip industry - ASML.

The Netherlands-based tech giant is the only company in the world able to build the machines needed to make the most sophisticated semiconductors.

Which is why ASML products will sit at the heart of the pilot line in Eindhoven - it's no coincidence that van Mol's project is based around the corner from ASML's headquarters.

"The way you produce these [photonic] chips is very similar to the way you produce electrical or electronic chip," says van Mol.

"You use the same type of equipment, you also need a high-end clean room, you also use wafers, so the production method is very similar to the traditional semiconductor technology."

ASML itself is keen to explore the opportunities that the emerging technology of photonics could offer.

"Europe has a strong position in photonics research. The next challenge is translating those innovations into industrial-scale manufacturing," says Stanislas Baron, who is the head of ASML's EU/US Customer Team.

ASML's unique success has helped build an influential and lucrative network of companies and institutions devoted to semiconductor technology in and around Eindhoven, and it's a model for what Europe is trying to achieve with photonic chips.

The Eindhoven project has the backing of former ASML chief executive Peter Wennink, author of an influential report for the Dutch government called The Roadmap to Future Prosperity , external , which noted that the market for photonics was expected to grow 10 to 20 times in the next 10 years.

In a news release backing the new pilot line, Wennink described it as "a launchpad for Europe's future digital economy".

"By investing in scalable production capacity, we are creating an ecosystem that can help shape the global technological direction," he said.

Of course, Europe is not alone in looking to the potential of photonics to earn a global economic advantage.

In June this year, US photonics company Coherent , external announced what it called "the world's first and largest volume-production six-inch indium phosphide manufacturing platform" at its plant in Sherman, in Texas.

The expansion is backed by chip manufacturing giant Nvidia, as well as $50 million public funds under the US Chips Act.

It's an illustration of how quickly the market is moving, and how central photonic chips could be to the continuing race to retain an influential stake in AI and technological development more generally.

Europe's bid to establish itself as a global leader in photonic chips – exemplified by the Eindhoven project – is the kind of strategy that makes sense in a globalised economy, says Joris Teer, policy analyst at the European Institute for Security Studies in Brussels.

If the continent can take a lead in photonic chips, then future developments in AI and data will partly be dependent on Europe.

"Europe knows that its high energy and labour costs, skilled workforce shortages, and lack of private and public capital make an across-the-board reindustrialisation strategy impossible", Teer says.

"To retain influence, ensuring dependence on European parties rather than European autonomy is key."…
